Travel demand does not spread evenly across the map. It gathers in a few famous places. "This imbalance — too many people in too few places — is at the heart of the problem, and it mirrors global travel patterns," Tim Oakes, managing director of Inside Travel Australia, told ABC News.

Industry observers note that the best-known names account for the largest share of that traffic, and New York alone received 65 million visitors in 2025, according to NYC Tourism + Conventions. When the most celebrated cities carry that much traffic, the people who live in them share their sidewalks, trains, and restaurant tables with a steady stream of outsiders. The more useful question in 2026 is not which city is the most exciting to visit. It is the cities that manage to work for visitors and residents at the same time.

It has been revealed that what makes a city pleasant to live in and what draws visitors often depend on different things, even when both look strong in the same year. A resident cares about the cost of a weeknight dinner, a park within walking distance, and a commute that works. A visitor weighs hotel rates, the cost of the trip in their home currency, and how crowded the famous sights will be.

Recent findings suggest that some of those conditions lie outside any city's control, such as hotels cutting prices to compete for fewer guests, visitors whose home currency is unusually strong, growing crowds, or a flood after heavy rain. A city may seem cheap, beautiful, or joyful this year, partly because of circumstances that could change by next year. The useful way to judge any city's standing is to ask what supports it and what could take that support away.

Sources indicate that time Out set out to find the world's best cities by balancing how much they appeal to visitors with how livable they are for the people who call them home, and it took in places as different as Cape Town, Seoul, Edinburgh, and Shanghai. Each city is there for its own reason, whether food, scenery, low prices, culture, or sheer excitement, and no two strike the balance between residents and visitors in the same way. For each one, the questions are: what sustains its strength, and what could upset that balance?

Industry observers note that the case for Melbourne, Australia, comes from the ordinary days of the people who live there, not from any single landmark. Time Out ranks Melbourne first among the world's cities, and the firmest evidence for that placement comes from locals, 94% of whom give high marks to the food they eat in their own city. Eating out is part of daily life for Melbourne residents, so a visitor mostly eats in the same places locals already use. What outsiders find in the city comes straight from what the people who live there enjoy. Young people deciding where to settle also think well of Melbourne, which places third worldwide as a home for Gen Z. That suggests its livability matters for the years ahead as well as for today.

Visitors have extra reasons to come in 2026, though those reasons belong to the calendar more than to daily life in the city. Fans broke attendance records at the Australian Open this year, and the NFL is set to stage its first regular-season game in Australia at the MCG. That game gives American football fans who might not otherwise consider a trip a reason to come. Both events depend on a schedule that changes from year to year, while the food and the everyday livability are there every week. Residents' daily life is therefore the steadier basis for Melbourne's standing.

It has been revealed that melbourne's case is weakest after dark. Seventy-seven percent of locals recommend the nightlife, and while that is a clear majority, fewer residents vouch for it than for the food. Residents and visitors share the city's newest rail link equally. Trains have begun running through the Metro Tunnel, and office workers and sightseers board the same line, so neither group gains at the other's expense.

According to recent reports, melbourne's everyday pleasures belong to residents and visitors alike, and that is why both groups are well served. Whether the excitement of this year's events lasts beyond 2026 is still an open question.

For the people who live in Shanghai, low prices are part of ordinary life. Shanghai posted the highest affordability score of any city, according to Time Out, and 88% of its residents call eating out cheap. For most of them, a meal out is a routine expense rather than a treat, and that stays true month after month for anyone who lives there. A visitor's biggest bill is usually a bed rather than a meal, though, and hotel prices depend on different forces.

According to recent reports, cheap meals do not mean cheap nights. Price competition among hotels was clear in Shanghai, as it was in Xinjiang and Yunnan, according to Trip.com data reported by CNBC. Even so, a median one-night stay costs 595 yuan (US$88), which is a real expense in a city where residents find dining out inexpensive. The same competition revealed up in regions far from Shanghai and very different from it, which suggests the pressure on hotel prices comes from forces larger than any one city. "While tourism is still a bright spot, [it] cannot escape this broad macro trend," Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis, said.

According to recent reports, foreign travelers are too small a group to hold up the travel market on their own, even as entry gets easier for some of them. Canadian and British travelers were approved for visa-free entry on February 15, but overseas visitors account for only 12% to 13% of tourism spending in China, according to a Natixis estimate reported by CNBC. The hotel market that visitors use therefore depends largely on domestic travelers, a different group from the residents who enjoy cheap meals.

According to recent reports, shanghai passes the affordability test for the people who live there today. For the people who visit, the value is real, but it rests on Chinese travelers and a wider economy that no single city controls.

It has been revealed that edinburgh's standing rests mostly on the people who live there rather than on the people who fly in. Contentment with ordinary life is close to universal among residents, and 91% of them say daily life in the city brings them joy, which puts Edinburgh among the happiest places surveyed, according to Time Out. The city also ties for the top walkability score, and those results help place Edinburgh third in the world. Residents give high marks to their parks and green spaces as well, and 94% of them approve of what they eat in their own city.

Industry observers note that edinburgh is easy to walk largely because it is small. VisitBritain indicates that a person can cover the entire city center on foot in a single day. Planners in a sprawling metropolis could not create that kind of compactness, however well they designed its streets. For a visitor, the small center means getting around the way a resident does, on foot, without having to learn a transit system.

According to recent reports, many outsiders come for the festivals, and VisitBritain counts 10 of international standing in the city. The Berliner Philharmoniker is opening the 2026 Edinburgh International Festival. Classical music fans who want to hear the orchestra have a reason to plan a trip around those particular dates on the calendar.

Good food, green space and short walks are there in every month, whether or not a festival is on.

Nearly every Londoner values the city's culture. Time Out reports that 99% of locals rate the city's culture scene highly, and that near-unanimity helps place London fourth. Time Out's own staff agreed with the residents, giving London the most votes in a tie with Tokyo. In London, the culture that tourists come for is the same culture that Londoners value in their own lives, so the city serves both groups at once.

Industry observers note that londoners will have three major latest museums to visit this year, and not all of them are in the old center. V&A East is opening in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, in East London, according to the Museums Association. V&A East is also working with young people as partners. Closer to the center, the London Museum is moving into the former Victorian General Market at Smithfield, and it will give an old market building a new use. Londoners in the east will gain a major museum close to where they live.

Londoners also rate their green space highly, with 94% of locals giving it high marks. Travelers $TRV hoping to see the London Museum in its latest home should keep their aims flexible. The museum is expected to open at Smithfield in the autumn, but the Museums Association describes the timing as approximate rather than fixed, and a trip built around a single day could miss it. That uncertainty matters little, because no single opening decides whether London deserves a visit. "You'd struggle to find a place more varied, idiosyncratic and exciting anywhere on earth," Joe Mackertich, Time Out's editor-in-chief for the U.K., stated.

For now, London pleases both its residents and its visitors, and the question for 2026 is whether its latest museums in the east and the center will win over Londoners as well as tourists.

According to recent reports, new Yorkers find their own city more thrilling than residents anywhere else find theirs. Some 78% of locals named New York the most exciting city in the world, according to Time Out, the highest share of any city by a wide margin. New York ranks fifth, and that excitement is what most sets it apart. The praise comes from people who live in the city day after day, not from tourists who see it for a weekend. What it leaves open is whether that thrill reaches the people who come to visit.

Sources indicate that foreign travelers have not answered that excitement with more trips. International arrivals fell 3.2% in 2025, according to NYC Tourism + Conventions, though the decline was smaller than forecast and visits from the U.K., Italy and Mexico rose. The pullback is modest, but it comes from a group that brings the city a large share of its tourism money. "The international visitor market is crucial to our economy, accounting for 50% of tourism spending," Julie Coker, president and CEO of Newly introduced York City Tourism + Conventions, noted. New York's appeal, therefore, rests on two separate groups. Residents supply the excitement, while foreigners whose numbers are wavering supply much of the tourism money.

It has been revealed that the city's tourism promoters expect a modest rebound. NYC Tourism + Conventions forecasts 66.3 million visitors in 2026, but that number is a projection from the organization that markets the city, not a count of arrivals. Nothing in it shows whether foreign travelers, a group so important to the city's tourism spending, will make up a larger share of those visitors.

New Yorkers have given their verdict on the city's excitement, and whether visitors from abroad will come back to share it remains an open question.

Industry observers note that the people who live in Cape Town, South Africa, make the strongest case for it, and they begin with the scenery they see every day. Locals rate the city's setting above every other city's, with 86% calling it the most beautiful, the top beauty score of any city, according to Time Out. That judgment comes from people who live beneath the mountain and beside the coast, not from visitors holding cameras. Cape Town ranks sixth in the world, and on the residents' side of the balance, its case rests on that regard for the city's beauty.

According to recent reports, visitors come for the price as much as for the view, and Europe supplies most of South Africa's overseas tourists. Selene Brophy, Senior Editor at Time Out South Africa, said that "if there’s one thing Cape Town does exceptionally well, it’s offer outstanding value for a world-class experience." Europeans made up 72.5% of overseas tourists to South Africa in February 2026, according to Cape Argus, while travelers from Asia accounted for only 7.1% of the country's overseas visitors that month. The country's tourism, and Cape Town's visitor trade with it, is therefore heavily tied to European travel.

That heavy reliance on Europe is the weak point in Cape Town's balance. Tensions in the Middle East could reduce the number of European tourists who make the trip, according to economist Dawie Roodt in comments reported by Cape Argus. No one in Cape Town has any say over that conflict, and residents' regard for their city does not depend on who flies in. Their love of its beauty is the steady half of Cape Town's appeal, and the flow of foreign visitors is the half that could change.

Cape Town clearly passes the test of being cherished by its own people, while the number of Europeans who keep coming to enjoy its value is the part still unsettled.

Industry observers note that the people of Mexico City value the people who make and sell things in their city above any monument. Residents give their small, independently owned stores and craftspeople higher marks than they give the food, and 85% of locals rate those shops and makers highly, according to Time Out.

Residents treat shopping in their city as part of their own lives, not as a trade set up for tourists. The city's food reputation also comes from people who eat there every day, and 80% of locals rate the dining scene highly. Mexico City ranks seventh out of 50 cities worldwide, and residents' high regard for their shops and food is part of what supports that standing. A visitor here largely uses the same city a resident does, eating at the same tables and buying from the same small shops.

According to recent reports, in 2026, people from far beyond the city will judge what its residents have built. Fans from around the world will come to Mexico City, a host city for the FIFA World Cup this year, and they will find the shops and dining rooms that locals already prize. The welcome offered to those fans rests on things residents value, though it leans more on food, culture, and nightlife than on the small makers locals rate highest. Mauricio Nava, Director Editorial of Time Out Mexico City, said, "we’re ready to welcome the world with our incredible gastronomy, culture and nightlife." Hosting a global crowd brings in newly introduced customers for the city's independent shops, and it also brings far more people who have never lived there.

Nobody can yet say whether the independent makers locals prize most will keep their local character once that crowd arrives.

According to recent reports, bangkok's appeal rests on how good an ordinary day feels to the people who live there, not on a skyline or a set of monuments. Asked about their daily routines, 79% of residents say those routines bring them joy, according to Time Out, and that contentment with ordinary days earns the city eighth place.

Recent findings suggest that much of that pleasure comes from eating, and 81% of residents rate the food scene highly. A visitor who eats where locals eat shares the same enjoyment. What travelers come for and what residents value are largely the same: good food and ordinary daily life.

It has been revealed that that kind of contentment depends on the city staying usable, and in late September 2026, much of it flooded. Nearly 300 millimeters of rain fell in 48 hours, ABC News reports, and the worst flooding was near the canals. About 4,200 people were staying in shelters, and for those households, the ordinary days that residents praised had stopped. The danger went well beyond spoiled looks. The flooding "poses a risk to people's lives," Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt stated. Knowing that residents are happy on a normal day reveals little about how safe and usable Bangkok is during a storm. That question now matters for anyone deciding whether to live in the city or travel there.

Visitors kept their main link to the outside world through the flood. Suvarnabhumi Airport remained in normal operation, according to ABC News, and flights could keep arriving and leaving while parts of the city were underwater. For a traveler, reaching Bangkok was easier than moving around the neighborhoods that took on water.

It has been revealed that bangkok passes the test of serving both residents and visitors on an ordinary day, but the outcome is not settled. No one can yet say how rapidly residents will get those days back.

Sources indicate that the people who live in Seoul, South Korea, and the people who judge cities for a living largely agree about it. Time Out reports that 79% of locals say Seoul makes them happy, so the city's appeal holds up for residents who live with it every day as well as for visitors. The experts who compare cities professionally reached the same verdict, tying Seoul for their third-favourite city. Those two verdicts rest on different grounds, which raises the question of what supports each one and whether they will stay aligned.

It has been revealed that A wave of cultural building is giving visitors a new reason to come to Seoul, and much of that building is in the capital. Four of the new cultural landmarks opening in South Korea in 2026 are in Seoul. The most prominent of them, the Centre Pompidou, is set to open this year in Seoul's 63 Building with funding from Hanwha Group's cultural foundation, according to Smithsonian. The museum's backers want Korean art to help shape the global conversation, not simply receive art from the West. The museum is "not intended as a one-way introduction of Western art, but as a reciprocal exchange in which Korean and Asian art can generate new interpretations and questions within global art discourse," a spokesperson for the Hanwha Foundation of Culture said. That aim matches the national plan, since South Korea has named 2026 its Year of Art. The Pompidou has not opened yet, though, so it gives visitors and experts something new without accounting for the happiness residents already report.

Large museum projects do not always win over the people who live near them. Residents of Busan, South Korea, protested a proposed museum project there over ecological concerns and cost, according to Smithsonian. The Busan protests show that residents can turn against a cultural project when they judge its cost or its effect on the environment to be too high.

Nothing suggests that Seoul's residents are turning against their city's latest museums. For now, the city's balance holds because locals and experts agree, and the test ahead is whether residents welcome the new landmarks or come to resent their cost.

Tokyo's young residents are happy with their city even as it fills with visitors. Among residents under 30, 91% say Tokyo makes them happy, according to Time Out. That figure is the verdict of the city's Gen Z residents, not of every Tokyoite, but it shows that Tokyo serves both the people who live there and the people who visit. That contentment earns Tokyo its place, and so far it has held up under the pressure that visitors bring.

According to recent reports, tokyo's crowds reached a new high in 2025, when the city set a record for international tourists. Those travelers gather in a few famous places rather than spreading out. Hayato Nagai, an associate professor at Ritsumeikan University Business School, says the strain is confined to certain spots and does not extend over the whole country. Tokyo has an extensive subway network, which Kyoto does not, ABC News reports, but Tokyo still sits with Kyoto, Osaka, and the area around Mount Fuji among the destinations under the heaviest pressure.

In a recent development, the pressure on Tokyo is likely to grow because Japan's government wants more visitors, not fewer. Only cars earn Japan more as an export than tourism does, ABC News reports, and officials aim to reach 60 million visitors by 2030, well beyond the record 42 million who came to Japan in 2025. With that much money at stake, the government has little reason to slow the boom. "Tokyo’s secret may be out, but the city remains a truly singular experience," Ili Saarinen, deputy editor of Time Out Tokyo, said. The distinct character Saarinen describes is the part of the city most exposed if Japan reaches its goal.

Tokyo passes the balance test today, and whether its young residents still feel as happy once Japan pursues its larger visitor goal remains an open question.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.
  • Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company noted.

Sources indicate that it works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the tech giant said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Sources indicate that noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

It has been revealed that choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A KFC franchisee's Chapter 11 filing puts stores in 10 states at risk. See what a listing means in each state, from Tennessee to Indiana.

It has been revealed that A large share of the KFC restaurants this franchisee may shut are in Tennessee. CBS 8 reports that 24 Tennessee locations are among the at-risk addresses. Those stores make up a sizable part of a closure list of more than 70 restaurants, according to Fast Tech giant. Within the state, the risk centers on one city: most of the listed addresses are in Memphis, Tenn., and the rest are spread across other Tennessee towns. That concentration shows where one owner happened to run its restaurants. It says nothing about how much Memphis diners want fried chicken, and a customer there is living through the owner's collapse more than a local downturn.

For Tennessee, much of the loss came before the bankruptcy did. Tasty Chick'n closed 19 Tennessee restaurants before it filed, according to Newsweek figures reported by Quartz. Those closures and the 24 listed locations come from separate counts that may not match address by address. The list itself mixes stores that are already closed or winding down with ones that are only unprofitable. Many of the state's losses happened before any judge was involved, and the stores still serving customers face an open question. A Tennessee diner who finds a familiar KFC on the list may be confirming a closing already noticed rather than learning of a new one.

Some of Florida's at-risk KFC stores may have closed before the bankruptcy began. CBS 8 reports that 11 Florida addresses are tied to leases the franchisee wants to exit, but the list does not say which of those stores are already closed. The manufacturer had shut 10 Florida restaurants before the filing, according to Newsweek figures reported by Quartz. Those two counts may overlap, so some listed Florida addresses could belong to restaurants that went dark months ago. For a Florida diner, the first question may be whether the local KFC is still open at all.

Sources indicate that it is not yet settled whether the bankruptcy will close any more Florida stores. A listing shows that the franchisee wants out of a lease. It does not confirm that a store still serving customers will shut. Tasty Chick'n looks a sale that could keep restaurants open under fresh owners, according to TheStreet, and that plan does not name any specific store for closing. A Florida store that is still operating could end up with a new operator rather than a locked door.

Industry observers note that kentucky's place in KFC's name gives its stores no protection from this franchisee's collapse. CBS 8 lists eight Kentucky addresses at risk, spread across Glasgow, Cave City, Madisonville, Mayfield, Murray, Owensboro, and Paducah, Ky., in a string of smaller regional cities rather than one metro area. Paducah has two of the listed stores, and the failure of a single owner can put more than one counter in the same town at risk. What links these towns is the tech giant that runs their restaurants, not anything happening in Kentucky's economy.

Kentucky holds only one part of a troubled operation. The Kentucky stores are operated by Tasty Chick'n LLC, a franchisee with 84 restaurants in all, according to Allrecipes. Nothing in the filing points to a weakness in Kentucky. The state appears because this operator happens to run stores there.

Alabama appears to have five KFC restaurants at risk, but the real number of restaurants is probably smaller. CBS 8 lists five Alabama addresses among the bankrupt franchisee's at-risk stores. The restaurant in Russellville, Ala., appears on that list twice with slightly different street wording, and Alabama Public Radio reports two Russellville addresses as well, so the five entries likely cover four restaurants. Four is the most Alabama could lose from this filing, not the number of stores expected to close.

It has been revealed that alabama's risk is confined to a few small towns in one corner of the state. The listed restaurants are in the north Alabama towns of Boaz, Arab, Hartselle and Russellville. None of the state's larger cities has a store on the list, so most Alabamians face no change at their local KFC from this bankruptcy. The cluster reveals where this one owner happened to run restaurants, not that north Alabama's economy is weaker than the rest of the state's.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the tech giant confirmed Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

In a recent development, guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company remarked. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the tech giant claims other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon remarked in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

In a recent development, breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The tech giant went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Sources indicate that fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in the United States and Canada have announced a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) revealed on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Industry observers note that importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," said Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

Tech Report: Radian Aerospace intends to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it aims to sell those materials to other companies as well.
  • Radian CEO Richard Humphrey noted he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it aims to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey noted he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey stated today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”.

Recent findings suggest that ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”.

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small tech giant.

Humphrey said the company right now has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

In a recent development, so, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey remarked. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”.

According to recent reports, he acknowledged that following through on the strategy for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he stated.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

It has been revealed that “It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”.

Industry observers note that is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace organization? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he noted. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This fall, my tech giant took an key message to the heart of Newly introduced York City.

In a recent development, the call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

Recent findings suggest that from working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search swiftly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

A newly introduced study we commissioned shows that nine times out of 10, AI directs shoppers to major retailers. Looking to buy a new road bike in New York? Chances are, ChatGPT will provide a list of national chains, even when there’s a great independent store just around the corner. The buyer didn’t ask for that kind of list. The model decided for them.

Sources indicate that for the past two decades, being discoverable online revolved around SEO. The basic question was: Are you showing up in Google results? Search engines learned shoppers’ locations and surfaced nearby businesses.

In a recent development, those priorities shouldn’t disappear just because answers now come from chatbots. If AI platforms are becoming the new front door to commerce, they share responsibility for which businesses get found.

According to recent reports, but small retailers can’t afford to wait for these companies to refine their search results. AI is changing the rules, and stores need to keep up. They have to think not only about whether search engines can find them, but whether AI understands who they are, what they sell, and why they’re worth recommending.

Recent findings suggest that one place to start is by educating customers. Our study found that adding words like “independent” or “locally owned” to AI searches reduced significant chains’ share of recommendations to as little as one in 10 on Google’s platforms.

Sources indicate that retailers can spread the word by sharing simple search tips with shoppers in-store, on their websites, and across social media. The more consumers make independent businesses a priority in their searches, the stronger the signal to AI companies that local options deserve greater visibility.

Beyond educating shoppers, here are three more things merchants can do to raise their profile in AI search.

It has been revealed that to get AI’s attention, small retailers also need to give them something to find. And the closer a shopper gets to making a purchase, the tougher the competition becomes. Our study showed that when someone names a specific product, a small store’s odds of being the top recommendation fall from roughly one in three to one in 10.

Sources indicate that significant retailers also have an advantage when it comes to how much information about them is readily available online. Their catalogs, inventory, product descriptions, reviews, and locations are already highly visible. Small merchants may have deeper expertise and better curation, but AI can’t recommend what it can’t see.

That makes it even more important for retailers to put their inventory online. AI agents increasingly fetch product information directly, which means retail websites may effectively become showrooms for both AI and human shoppers.Here, AI is part of the solution. New tools let retailers showcase their entire product catalog so agents can find what they’re looking for. Besides syncing that inventory with your POS, they write descriptions that make those products easier for AI to discover.

Making a retail website simple for AI to read is critical, too. Behind the scenes, a merchant can clearly label product details like price, brand, and whether an item is in stock, while also giving search and AI crawlers a map of the pages it wants them to find.

Industry observers note that when shoppers use an AI chatbot to search, they ask a lot of questions. What jacket styles are hot this fall? Which supportive running shoes are best for beginners? What are the top ergonomic office chairs for working from home?

For independent retailers, that creates another opportunity to get noticed. The key is to establish yourself as an expert by building authority around what you sell.

Useful, substantive content can help. For example, a bike shop could create TikTok or YouTube videos showing how to set up tubeless tires or replace a worn chain. Those clips may look educational, but what they’re really doing is showing the expertise behind the business.

Recent findings suggest that of all the social platforms, YouTube could be an independent merchant’s best friend. Just ask the small luxury watch dealers who use long-form informational videos to build trust — by exploring topics like how to avoid buying a fake.

According to recent reports, youTube’s connection to Google makes it an even more powerful tool for independent retailers. Gemini regularly surfaces videos from the site, giving merchants another way to get their expertise (and products) in front of shoppers using AI search.

A steady stream of blog posts can do the same thing. By posting weekly about fashion trends, for instance, a women’s clothing boutique gives AI systems more proof that it knows its category inside and out.

Industry observers note that if that sounds like a heavy lift, it doesn’t need to be. AI assistants can help write, publish, and manage blog content, while built-in SEO tools help optimize each post for traditional search and make it easier for search engines to crawl and AI systems to understand.

To stand out in AI search, small retailers also need to rethink what social media is for.

It has been revealed that platforms like Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube still help stores reach shoppers. But they now do a second job: showing AI what a business sells, what it knows, and what it specializes in.

According to recent reports, AI tools are paying attention. Social posts appear in almost 70% of Google’s AI Overview responses. And in Google’s AI mode, they show up in almost half of responses to searches that don’t name a brand — the ones shoppers type before they know your store exists.Meta’s fresh Muse agent takes this further. Muse works inside Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, which reach 3.6 billion people a day. With a shopper’s permission, it can learn their taste from what they follow, like, save, and share. Every customer who engages with a store’s posts is teaching their agent that the store belongs on their shortlist. Retailers with active, engaged communities are more likely to be recommended.

Industry observers note that that’s the real opening for local retailers: AI remembers what shoppers like. Once a customer shows their agent they value a certain kind of store, like a neighborhood bookshop or an independent boutique, it can keep recommending similar places.

For their part, retailers should show up consistently where both shoppers and AI are paying attention. By embracing this new reality, they can turn a potential threat into a reason for customers to make the trip.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ella Langley won 6 of 9 nominations, Taylor Swift returned after 13 years, and a piano caught fire. 9 moments from the 2026 CMA Awards.

Sources indicate that country music keeps score of its biggest night in trophies, but the 2026 Country Music Association Awards will be remembered for moments that often had nothing to do with winning. More than 7,000 voters chose this year's winners, according to CBC. Those voters belong to the Country Music Association, so their ballots record the industry's own choices rather than the moments that people in the arena and viewers at home will remember. This year one young singer collected far more of their awards than anyone else, while some of the genre's best-known names left without a trophy. That leaves two separate accounts of the night, one of who won and one of what people saw, and the two rarely match.

The second account is full of loss. Performers honored two country legends who died in 2026, and one winner devoted his trophy to his late mother. The stars also kept turning up in one another's moments. The host opened the show with a joke aimed at a guest, two singers set an old feud to music, and a veteran who won nothing in her own name had helped make a younger rival's winning record. Because so many of the night's artists were tied together, the ones who went home empty-handed often shaped the winners' night. A count of trophies leaves out most of what happened.

According to recent reports, yahoo set out to highlight the standout moments from the 2026 country music awards night, from a pop superstar's return to the CMA stage and a piano set on fire during a performance to a newcomer who took a long road into the genre and the biggest star to go home without a trophy. Some of the people in those moments won several trophies, and some won none. Each moment belongs to both stories at once: who collected the awards and who held the room's attention. Again and again, the same people shaped both.

Recent findings suggest that ella Langley set a single-night record at the CMA Awards, and she began collecting trophies the moment the show started. Of the nine awards she was up for, she took home six, Entertainer of the Year among them, according to Yahoo. Single of the year was the first award handed out, CBC reports, and she won it before going on to take the genre's highest honor. Voters picked her in most of her races, from honors for a single song to the evening's top award.

One record accounted for three of those trophies. Voters named "Choosin' Texas" the year's top music video and top song as well as its best single. The song had already dominated the charts, holding No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 longer than any other song and breaking a record Mariah Carey's holiday song had held, according to CBC. Those wins show voters rewarding a hit the public had already made clear it loved.

Recent findings suggest that langley understood how much of the night had become about her. "At this point, I'm sick of me!" she remarked as she accepted Entertainer of the Year. The joke admitted that the room had watched her walk to the stage again and again, and it kept the sweep from feeling like a coronation.

Industry observers note that langley is only 27, CBC reports, yet she already judged her career in the largest terms. She told the crowd that stopping now would still leave her with the best career of her life. Her next test is already set. Langley heads into the 69th Grammy Awards with seven nominations, ABC7 reports, and a different set of voters will judge her work there.

Sources indicate that taylor Swift came back to country music's biggest stage after a long absence, and she brought more country into her set than she had at her last visit. Swift had not performed at the CMA Awards in 13 years, Yahoo reports, and this set marked her return to that stage. At that earlier appearance she sang an acoustic "Red," according to ABC7, while this time Keith Urban played banjo beside her. With Urban on banjo, she staged the return as a full country homecoming rather than a quiet guest spot.

Sources indicate that her setlist placed her newest work beside the start of her country story. Swift sang a two-song medley that paired "I Knew It, I Knew You," from Toy Story 5, with one of her earliest country songs. The older pick was "Our Song," a track she had not sung on the CMA stage since 2007, according to ABC7. By pairing them, she told the room that her country beginnings are still part of the artist she is now. The film song indicated where she stands today, and the older one carried the homecoming.

Industry observers note that swift's return was never built around winning. She had a single nomination, for single of the year, and for her the night was a chance to perform rather than to compete. That category went to Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas," and Swift left without a trophy. The critics still put her at the top. She gave the best of the night's 15 performances, according to Billboard. The voters and the critics reached opposite verdicts on the same artist, and no one at the show made the gap between who won and what people saw plainer than Swift.

The show treated her as one of its own even though she won nothing. Organizers gave her the honor of handing Brooks & Dunn the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award, and that assignment marked her as a member of the country family rather than a guest from pop. Host Lainey Wilson also teased her from the stage the way a family teases a relative, and her target was Swift's July wedding to Travis Kelce. The wedding took place at Madison Square $SQ Garden, according to ABC7. "I never promised you Madison Square Garden," Wilson sang.

The trophies went to others, but much of the room's attention stayed on Swift.

According to recent reports, kacey Musgraves went into the 2026 CMA Awards with five nominations and came out with no trophies, according to Yahoo. Her duet with Miranda Lambert, "Horses and Divorces," was nominated as well, and Yahoo Entertainment reports that the award went to a different collaboration, so even the song she shared with Lambert left without a win. People will remember her night for the moment she stood onstage beside Lambert, and the history between the two singers is what gave that performance its weight.

That history began with a song Musgraves helped write for another singer. Yahoo Entertainment reports that Musgraves co-wrote "Mama's Broken Heart," which Lambert recorded in 2011 and took into the top 10 of Billboard's Country Airplay chart. Musgraves had her own breakthrough with "Merry Go 'Round" three years after Lambert's recording. By the time Musgraves broke through under her own name, a song she co-wrote had already become a hit for Lambert. The strain between the two grew out of that song, and the duet was their attempt to settle it.

Industry observers note that musgraves values the duet for feeling true to life. "I mean, it's real and that's why I love this song, because it's not coming from some contrived place in a writing room," Musgraves remarked, as reported by Yahoo Entertainment. Onstage, Lambert wore a belt buckle that referenced "Middle of Nowhere," a Musgraves album, according to Yahoo. The singer who once took a Musgraves song to the radio wore a tribute to Musgraves's own work. Viewers at home heard only part of the song, because multiple lyrics were bleeped on the broadcast.

The arena heard the reconciliation in full, and the voters gave it nothing.

Country Music Association voters gave their award for newcomers to a man who had already lost the same race once. Stephen Wilson Jr. was 47 when he won New Artist of the Year, according to Yahoo. WHAS11 reports that this was his second nomination for the award and that he had never won a CMA Award before. The category meant to announce discoveries ended up handing a patient contender his first trophy.

Industry observers note that wilson Jr. came to country music by a long detour, and that path helps explain his age on the night he won. Before music, he worked as a food scientist. WHAS11 reports that he also boxed as an amateur and that, once he turned to songs, he wrote for Tim McGraw. On awards night he sang "I'm a Song" alongside Chris Stapleton. He came to the award having already written songs for one of country's best-known stars. The trophy introduced his own name to the wider audience, but it did not mark his first work in country music.

It has been revealed that wilson Jr. turned to music after his father's death, according to WHAS11. His thanks on accepting the award described a real change of course rather than a stock line. "Thank you country music for changing my life," Wilson Jr. said. Voters gave the night's award for newly introduced talent to an artist who took one of the least traditional paths into the genre, and that choice highlights their vote can reward persistence as readily as youth.

The tributes to Dolly Parton and John Anderson gave the night some of its strongest emotion, even though neither artist could compete for anything. Yahoo reports that both icons died in 2026 and were honored with emotional tributes on stage. The industry gathered to mourn a loss from earlier in the same year, since Dolly died in August, according to Yahoo News. The Anderson tribute also put one of the industry's earlier decisions back on stage. Zach Top and Dierks Bentley sang "Swingin'," the song that earned Anderson the CMA's Single of the Year in 1983. In that performance, the record of who won and the memory people carried home from the night were the same thing, and the honor had been settled decades before this year's vote.

Industry observers note that dolly's farewell opened the broadcast before any trophy was handed out. Yahoo News reports that the opening tribute was "I Will Always Love You," sung by Vince Gill and host Lainey Wilson, while Yahoo reports that Stephen Wilson Jr. was the singer beside Gill. Both accounts agree on Gill, so whichever Wilson joined him, a veteran of the genre led the goodbye.

According to recent reports, the remembrance carried onto the red carpet, where Dolly's niece, Danielle Parton, wore a gown designed for Dolly that she never wore, according to Yahoo News. "They poured me into it tonight, and I'm gonna do my best to honor her wearing it," said Parton, who is also brand ambassador for Dolly's estate.

Recent findings suggest that dolly's music remains up for honors beyond this one night. The 2026 version of her song "Light of a Clear Blue Morning," recorded with Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Reba McEntire and Queen Latifah, is nominated for the Grammy for Best Country Duo/Group Performance, according to Yahoo News. The room said goodbye to Dolly while one of her recordings was still in contention for another award.

The winner with the most familiar result gave the night its most private moment. Chris Stapleton collected his ninth Male Vocalist award, according to Yahoo. Few results that evening surprised anyone less. He turned that repeat into a tribute to his mother, who died a year earlier. "She always told me I could be anything I wanted to be," Stapleton stated, as reported by WOKQ. Her words cast nine trophies as proof of something she believed long before he won any of them. His grief made the most predictable win of the night one of its most memorable.

His trophy came from years of loyal voters, not from a single big night. His first Male Vocalist award came in 2015, according to WOKQ, and this latest one capped more than a decade in which CMA members kept picking his voice. On the same night that those members gave Ella Langley a record haul, they still kept rewarding Stapleton. They celebrated one artist's huge year and stayed loyal to a familiar singer at the same time. Next to a one-night sweep, his result reveals how far staying power can carry a career.

Industry observers note that stapleton also used the stage to look ahead. He debuted "I'm a Song," a new track with Stephen Wilson Jr., who joined him to perform it. The trophy went to one man, but two artists shared the moment.

Nine trophies in, Stapleton is still bringing fresh songs to the stage, and his run looks far from finished.

Lainey Wilson spent her first minutes as host making Taylor Swift part of the show before Swift sang a note. Wilson could take that liberty because she knew the stage well. Yahoo reports that she emceed the CMA Awards for a third straight year and opened by singing, with Brad Paisley, a number that teased Swift about her wedding. The teasing came across as affection because it came from inside Swift's own circle. Swift married Travis Kelce in July, according to Parade, and Paisley was a guest at the couple's wedding celebration. Swift laughed at the joke from the audience.

Industry observers note that wilson built the joke on a country standard. She changed a line from Lynn Anderson's "Rose Garden" so that it pointed to Madison Square $SQ Garden instead. Anderson took that song to the top of Billboard's Hot Country Singles chart in 1970, so Wilson welcomed pop's biggest star back with one of the genre's own hits.

According to recent reports, wilson had her own standing to joke about weddings. Yahoo reports that she married earlier in 2026, and she set her ceremony beside Swift's as country's plainer version. "What are you talking about arena? I got married in a cave!" Wilson noted, as reported by Parade. The gag made Swift's homecoming feel like a reunion among friends, and Wilson was one of them.

The Swift joke was only one part of a larger act. The opening routine also included a parody of Loretta Lynn's "Coal Miner's Daughter," according to Parade. Wilson and Paisley turned another classic from the genre's canon into a joke about the present. Wilson hosts through musical comedy with a partner rather than stand-up patter.

Before anyone opened an envelope, she had shown the room a night where country's stars and its history kept turning up in one another's moments.

Sources indicate that tucker Wetmore gave the night one of its most striking images from behind a piano. He played inside a ring of flames while the instrument itself burned, according to Yahoo. A strong set stood behind the spectacle. Billboard ranks his performance second of the night's 15, behind only Taylor Swift, which put him close to the night's biggest star in a critic's eyes. That standing reflects Billboard's judgment of what he did onstage, not an award or a vote. Wetmore earned his place among the night's moments through what people saw rather than through who won.

Wetmore sang his own song before he moved to the burning piano. He opened with "Who Told You That," his own song, backed by a horn section, according to Billboard. The room heard who he is as a singer before any fire appeared. He then sat down at the piano for "All My Rowdy Friends (Are Coming Over Tonight)," a Hank Williams Jr. song, and he played that cover as the piano burned.

The fire that people remember from Wetmore's set came with another man's song rather than his own.

Country music voters turned Miranda Lambert away and rewarded her work on the same night. Lambert lost in all three categories in which she was nominated, according to Yahoo, and went home without a trophy of her own. Voters still gave the album award to Ella Langley's "Dandelion," and ABC7 reports that Lambert co-produced that record. The same membership judged her name and her work separately and reached opposite answers.

An empty night means more for an artist whom this room has honored for years. Lambert has won 14 CMA Awards over her career, according to Yahoo Entertainment. This year, the only work of hers that voters rewarded was work she had done for another singer. Her part in Langley's success also reaches into the songs themselves. She was a producer and a co-writer on "Choosin' Texas," so part of the song behind Langley's rise came from Lambert's own writing. Lambert helped make both the winning album and the night's biggest song, and that ties her shutout to Langley's breakout.

In a recent development, lambert did not spend the night on the edges of the broadcast. She performed twice. She and Langley used part of that stage time to sing "Snakeskin Boots" on television for the first time. The performance shows the two singers working together beyond the winning album.

Lambert lost all three of her own races and still left the stage after debuting new music with the woman who won.

Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.
  • Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup released by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of owners in its invite-only beta.
  • In a recent development, that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup released by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of owners in its invite-only beta.

In a recent development, that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Industry observers note that vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, mentioned last month that it intends to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo debuted last month, Fridgen mentioned it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo states no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s latest booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister tech giant Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Industry observers note that vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever organization they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo owners get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

Sources indicate that the service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

Sources indicate that his co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the tech giant notes it prepares to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the slowed performance witnessed across the XRP ETF market in recent weeks, it appears that interest in the investment product remains intact especially through its largest issuer, Bitwise.

In a recent 13F filings with the U.S. SEC, the national bank of Canada, revealed it recently joined the XRP ETF ecosystem, showcasing its exposure to XRP through the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Although the bank did not disclose the specific amount it had invested in the asset, the filing has triggered discussions as it highlights XRP’s growing exposure among institutional investors.

In a recent development, notably, the Form 13F the bank filed with the SEC covers the third quarter of 2026, which ended on September 30. This suggests that it had recently joined the XRP ecosystem despite the prolonged market weakness.

Unlike regular investors who purchase XRP directly from exchanges and hold in their wallets, the bank invested in XRP through Bitwise's fund.

With its XRP ETF offering, Bitwise allows traditional investors to gain exposure to XRP without having to manage the crypto asset themselves.

Although XRP has continued to see major institutions and banks join its ETF ecosystem, participation in the XRP funds have slowed significantly following the ongoing market volatility.

While the exposure showcased by the major Canadian bank highlights growing XRP ETF adoption, it doesn’t change the fact that institutional traders are beginning to take caution as they have just recorded the highest weekly withdrawals since March 2026.

The bank’s XRP exposure has triggered discussions as it reveals that it has retained its position till September 30 despite the persisting market correction.

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and indicates it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

It has been revealed that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and indicates it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

In a recent development, the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It states TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

Industry observers note that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It indicates TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Recent findings suggest that here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

It has been revealed that gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

It has been revealed that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Recent findings suggest that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card states AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Industry observers note that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card demonstrates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a significant generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 upcoming tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Recent findings suggest that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Industry observers note that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

Industry observers note that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.
