This 54-Year-Old Left Her Full-Time Therapist Job to Focus on a Flavorful Side Hustle Making $10K a Month on Amazon: ‘I Used ChatGPT’

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lana Wimmer, 54, of St.
  • Industry observers note that when did you launch the side hustle, and what specific consumer pain point did you want to address?
  • My husband and I had lived in Europe and the Middle East, where we’d discovered nonalcoholic fruit malt beverages with this wonderful depth, body and flavor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lana Wimmer, 54, of St. George, Utah. She started her side hustle Öl Brew (pronounced “cool” without the “c”), a nonalcoholic sparkling fruit malt beverage, while working about 40 hours a week as a mental health therapist. Once she caught herself sitting in a therapy session thinking about Öl Brew, she knew she had to focus on the business full-time. The brand generates about $10,000 a month in revenue on Amazon. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Industry observers note that when did you launch the side hustle, and what specific consumer pain point did you want to address? We launched Öl Brew in 2026, about six months ago, but the idea had been with me for eight years. For most of that time, I kept hoping someone else would make these drinks. I had absolutely no ambition to enter the beverage industry.

My husband and I had lived in Europe and the Middle East, where we’d discovered nonalcoholic fruit malt beverages with this wonderful depth, body and flavor. They were nothing like the sodas we had back home. When we returned to the U.S., I couldn’t find anything that compared. The options felt uninspired: soda, sparkling water or a mocktail trying awfully hard to replace alcohol. I didn’t want an imitation of something else. I wanted a genuinely different drinking experience.

It has been revealed that how did you validate that people would actually pay for your solution before investing serious money?One evening, I finally shared my idea over dinner with friends. The response was immediate. Everyone wanted better nonalcoholic options; this wasn’t just my personal preference.

Industry observers note that I was also watching a shift in consumer behavior, particularly among my own adult children and their friends. They weren’t gathering around alcohol. They were cold plunging, working out and training for HYROX competitions. Their social lives looked different, and so did their beverage choices. Having spent decades as a therapist, I was especially interested in what was driving that shift. People were becoming more intentional about how they spent their time, what they consumed and how they connected.

Those early conversations gave me the conviction to invest although they weren’t proof of purchase. That came later when we got the product onto shelves and watched customers respond. Sometimes you recognize a gap in the market because you’ve been standing in it for years.

It has been revealed that which two or three essential tools, apps or pieces of gear did you buy in your first week, and which ones did you skip to save money?My first tools were a notebook, my computer and ChatGPT. I started writing down everything I wanted to build, followed by a much longer list of everything I didn’t know.

Recent findings suggest that I used ChatGPT to research flavor houses, co-packers, brand management companies, distributors and how the beverage industry actually works. It helped me learn the terminology, understand the process and figure out whom I needed to talk to. But the real education came when I started taking those questions to people with experience. AI gave me a starting point. Industry professionals gave me context, perspective and occasionally some very expensive lessons.

Industry observers note that I also listened constantly to business and beverage podcasts, particularly The Game with Alex Hormozi, Tim Bush’s On the Shelf and Joey Pedone’s Sippin’ & Selling. I didn’t spend money on elaborate software systems or expensive subscriptions in the beginning. My priority was understanding the business well enough to make informed decisions. I learned quickly that information is relatively easy to find. Knowing what to do with it is another matter entirely.

What were the first three steps you took in your first 30 days?My first 30 days were focused on three things: Developing a go-to-market plan, identifying our target consumer and first four flavors, and finding the people who could help bring the product to life.

In a recent development, I used AI to help research the industry and build an initial strategy. Then I settled on apple, lemon, peach and pomegranate as our first flavors. I wanted something familiar enough that people would be curious to try it, but different enough that they’d immediately recognize this wasn’t ordinary soda.

Recent findings suggest that then came the investment. I spent $50,000 hiring a beverage development company to help formulate the drinks and connect us with a co-packer. I also hired a branding company to develop our can designs and brand book. Altogether, the initial upfront cost, including the pilot run and production run, was about $200,000.

Here’s what I learned later: The formulation work could have been arranged without that fee. I didn’t know that at the time. That was an expensive introduction to an industry where relationships, experience and knowing the right questions to ask can save you a tremendous amount of money.

It has been revealed that how did you land your first paying customer?Our first paying customer came after our pilot run and initial production, and there was nothing sophisticated about the sales strategy. We walked into a local grocery store, sat down with the manager, introduced ourselves and told him what we were building. He agreed to carry Öl Brew.

Another local farmers market retailer followed, and suddenly our drinks were on shelves, where actual customers could decide if our idea had merit. Those first accounts gave us more than revenue. They gave us feedback, credibility and the opportunity to start building a business in the real world.

Recent findings suggest that after all the planning, design, and money we’d spent, our first sale came from sitting across a table and having a conversation. I rather love that.

Sources indicate that nowadays, which specific tools or platforms help you bring in customers, and what is one feature inside those tools that saves you the most time?We’re using Instagram, TikTok Shop, Amazon, Walmart.com and our Shopify website to introduce consumers to Öl Brew and drive sales. Because we’re bringing an entirely latest beverage experience to the American market, our marketing has to do more than create awareness. We have to give people a reason to be curious. Most consumers understand soda. They understand sparkling water. But sparkling fruit malt soda? That’s a conversation starter.

On the operational side, Klaviyo has been particularly useful for automating customer communication through Shopify. We can capture email addresses, create welcome sequences, share promotions and maintain relationships without manually managing every interaction. That kind of automation matters when you’re running lean.

According to recent reports, what was the single biggest bottleneck that almost stalled your business, and what exact change or process fixed it?Distribution has been our biggest challenge. The beverage industry has a complicated relationship between retailers and distributors. Retailers want to know who’s distributing your product. Distributors increasingly want retail authorizations before they’ll take on a new brand. Which leaves emerging brands trying to convince both sides to move first.

We would attend trade shows and return with interest from eight distributors across the country. The conversations were promising, the enthusiasm was real, and then everything would stall because we didn’t yet have the retail commitments to support distribution. It was frustrating and forced us to reconsider our approach.

Industry observers note that we realized we needed to focus less on how many distributors were interested and more on securing actual retail placements. That meant targeting independent stores and smaller retailers more willing to take a chance on something new. We also brought on an experienced VP of sales to help sharpen our strategy, prioritize accounts and build a more disciplined approach to retail expansion. It’s a significant shift, and we’re beginning to see a clearer path forward.

Industry observers note that how many months did it take to reach consistent monthly revenue, and what was your average monthly profit during your first six months?We’re still working toward consistent monthly revenue. We’re only a few months into launch, and building a beverage brand requires significant capital long before the revenue catches up. But we’ve had encouraging early traction.

During Sober October, Öl Brew reached No. 14 in a nonalcoholic beverage ranking on Amazon. We also generated approximately $10,000 in Amazon revenue during October, just months after launching on the platform.

We’re not yet consistently profitable. We’re investing in inventory, marketing, distribution and the team we need to support growth. There’s a part of entrepreneurship that rarely makes it into the success stories: the period when you’re spending money, making adjustments and trying to determine which investments will actually produce results. That’s where we are.

What is your current monthly revenue and profit margin? We’re about six months into launch, with Amazon generating approximately $10,000 in monthly revenue, plus additional sales through retail and other ecommerce channels. We’re still investing heavily in growth, so we haven’t established a consistent net profit margin.

In a recent development, what part of the work do you still handle yourself, and which tasks have you outsourced?As for my time, I spend roughly 10 hours a day on Öl Brew, often more. My work falls into three main areas: brand awareness, retail and distribution, and manufacturing and operations. We’ve outsourced Amazon optimization and SEO, TikTok Shop management and creator partnerships, and much of our branding, marketing and social media execution.

Industry observers note that if someone is starting from scratch today, what are common beginner mistakes they should avoid?Don’t rush into hiring. I made the mistake of trusting people who promised far more than they could deliver. Some were convincing, experienced and very good at selling their services. I was excited about building the brand, and that excitement sometimes made me move faster than I should have.

Now, I recommend interviewing at least three to five people or companies before making a significant hire. The interview process itself is an education. You’ll hear different strategies, cost structures and perspectives on what’s possible. Eventually, you’ll begin to recognize who understands the work and who simply knows how to sell it.

In a recent development, and don’t confuse confidence with having all the answers. I started a beverage company at 54 after a career in mental health. I knew a great deal about people and relationships. I knew very little about beverage manufacturing, distribution or retail. That experience has been both humbling and energizing. What I brought into this business wasn’t industry expertise. It was curiosity, conviction and a willingness to learn. I still believe those are some of the most valuable things an entrepreneur can have.

Be ambitious about what you want to build. Just be equally discerning about who you trust to help you build it.

Your Business Is Saving Hours With AI. So Why Are Customers Still Waiting?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.
  • Recent findings suggest that we needed access to the client’s digital platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

Recent findings suggest that we needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission problems, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

In a recent development, I’ve encountered different versions of this problem throughout my consulting career. Teams have the expertise. The technology exists. Everyone wants to move forward. Yet progress stalls because the underlying process is more complicated than anyone realized.

It made me think about how businesses are approaching artificial intelligence. We’re investing in tools that promise to make work faster, but how often do we stop to examine what’s slowing the business down in the first place?

In a recent development, when entrepreneurs think about productivity, they naturally focus on the time employees spend completing tasks. How swiftly can we produce a report? How much time can we save creating content? Can AI respond to routine inquiries? Those are reasonable questions.

But consider what happened in the healthcare project. Automating another task wouldn’t have resolved who owned the account, who could authorize access or how the team should handle authentication. Those were process and accountability problems.

This is why I believe every business should examine its workflows before investing heavily in automation.

It has been revealed that I’ve previously written about why entrepreneurs should examine workflows before hiring more employees. The same principle applies to technology.

If responsibilities are unclear and information is scattered, automation may simply help a flawed process move faster.

A business owner might celebrate saving 20 hours a week. The customer is asking a different question: Why am I still waiting?

That gap is easy to overlook because internal performance metrics don’t always reflect the customer experience.

Sources indicate that imagine improving the speed of customer service responses while leaving the underlying resolution process unchanged. Customers might receive answers sooner but still wait days for their problems to be addressed.

The business reports an efficiency improvement. Customers experience little difference. I see a similar disconnect in marketing. Companies sometimes invest in generating more leads without examining what happens after those leads arrive.

As I explored in my article about why businesses can spend more on marketing while attracting fewer customers, more activity doesn’t automatically translate into better commercial results. The lesson applies to AI as well.

Measure the outcome, not just the activity that produced it.

One thing I’ve learned from managing complex projects is that technology cannot replace clear ownership. Someone still needs to make decisions, resolve exceptions and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

Before automating a process, I ask three questions:.

If those answers aren’t clear, technology isn’t the first thing I would fix.

It has been revealed that for example, automated appointment reminders can reduce administrative effort. But if patients cannot easily reschedule or reach someone when they need help, the experience remains frustrating.

Recent findings suggest that the same is true for sales, onboarding and service delivery. Customers appreciate convenience, but they also want confidence that someone is paying attention.

This may be the most important question entrepreneurs should ask about AI.

Saving time is only valuable when businesses put that time to better use. This is the AI productivity trap: Faster work doesn’t necessarily mean faster growth. The real opportunity lies in using that efficiency to improve customer relationships, solve problems and create measurable business value.

Suppose a new system saves your team 10 hours every week. What do you do with that time? Do you reinvest it in customer relationships? Improve service quality? Reduce expenses? Give employees more opportunities to solve problems that technology cannot handle?

Or does that time simply disappear into additional meetings and administrative work? The answer matters.

It has been revealed that in my earlier Entrepreneur article about why business growth doesn’t always improve profitability, I discussed the importance of looking beyond top-line results. Productivity deserves the same scrutiny.

An efficient business isn’t necessarily a profitable one, and a productive team isn’t automatically delivering a better customer experience.

Entrepreneurs need to decide how efficiency gains will create value before assuming they will.

My advice is simple: Choose one process that repeatedly creates problems. It might be customer onboarding, appointment scheduling, account access, proposal approvals or resolving support requests. Follow that process from beginning to end.

It has been revealed that talk to the people involved. Identify where information gets lost, approvals stall or responsibilities become unclear. Then ask whether the problem requires automation at all.

In a recent development, sometimes the answer is a better system. Sometimes it’s eliminating an unnecessary approval. Sometimes it’s giving one person clear responsibility for following through.

Make one change, measure what happens, and expand what works. You may discover that the most valuable improvement costs considerably less than another software subscription.

I’m enthusiastic about what AI can do for entrepreneurs, especially smaller businesses competing with organizations that have significantly greater resources. But I don’t believe adopting more technology automatically makes a company more competitive.

The healthcare project reinforced something I’ve seen repeatedly: Even capable teams with good technology can struggle when the underlying process isn’t working.

Your customers don’t see how many hours you save internally. They notice whether you deliver what you promised, respond when they need you and make their lives easier.

Before celebrating how much faster your business has become, make sure your customers can feel the difference.

Tech Report: Waymo states its robotaxis crash far less than humans. California just called them an ‘imminent hazard’ and pulled them off freeways

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that waymo states its robotaxis are involved in far fewer serious crashes than human drivers.
  • 11, the California Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo from operating or testing its driverless cars on freeways after several vehicles entered an active construction closure and another incident in which a Waymo tried to get around California Highway Patrol cars running a traffic break.
  • “Right now we’re looking at this technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that waymo states its robotaxis are involved in far fewer serious crashes than human drivers. California regulators now say its cars are an “imminent hazard” on the freeway.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 11, the California Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo from operating or testing its driverless cars on freeways after several vehicles entered an active construction closure and another incident in which a Waymo tried to get around California Highway Patrol cars running a traffic break. Waymo has since paused driverless freeway rides in all its markets, including Phoenix, Miami and Austin, though it is still testing on freeways with specialists behind the wheel.

“Right now we’re looking at this technology. You get in it, you expect it to work perfectly,” Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT’s AgeLab who studies automated vehicles, told Fortune. “We shouldn’t.”.

According to recent reports, the DMV said three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame on Nov. 5. Then the agency cited the separate incident involving Highway Patrol vehicles in San Francisco, ultimately resulting in the agency declaring Waymo’s freeway operations an “imminent hazard to public safety,” in a statement.

It has been revealed that it’s the second time this year Waymo’s freeway service has gone dark. Similar incidents in May prompted an earlier restriction and corrective actions, but the DMV said Waymo’s vehicles continued entering active construction zones despite those changes. Waymo paused freeway rides nationwide then, too, and brought them back gradually starting in late July.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” a Waymo spokesperson told Fortune, adding that the recent incidents did not result in any injuries or collisions.

California’s restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can show regulators that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway hazards. The company notes it’s working with officials to get back on freeways, though winning public confidence may be a less straightforward process.

Waymo’s robotaxis are still operating on surface streets, where the tech giant claims it provides more than half a million rides each week. The company began offering passengers freeway trips in California in November 2025, after years of autonomous freeway driving.

Waymo, however, does have numbers to make its case. Across more than 270 million fully autonomous miles through June, the company says its cars have been involved in 82% fewer injury-causing crashes and 95% fewer crashes causing serious injuries or worse than statistically comparable human drivers. Waymo also says its vehicles have been involved in 93% fewer injury-causing crashes involving pedestrians.

It has been revealed that but Reimer cautioned that those numbers don’t necessarily tell the whole story. Waymo’s software and vehicles are constantly changing, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about a technology that may look different today than it did when many of those miles were recorded.

Even if the numbers hold up, being safer than human drivers may not be enough to convince Americans to hop in the back of the baby-blue Waymo.

“Humans look at robots to be better than human, and I think the same is true for automated vehicles,” he mentioned.

Reimer sees human drivers as a reasonable starting point for measuring safety, but as robotaxis expand, he believes they’ll need to clear a much higher bar.

“If you’re going to expand, it’s gotta be magnitudes safer,” he remarked.

Sources indicate that reimer argues that part of the problem is how autonomous driving has been presented to the public. A Waymo might have an empty driver’s seat, but that doesn’t mean humans are entirely out of the picture. Remote support staff can step in to help when vehicles encounter problems.

Recent findings suggest that “It is not autonomous driving,” Reimer said. “It is highly automated, but there is a lot of human components behind the scenes.”.

He believes companies could earn more trust by being upfront about those limitations instead of treating the technology like a finished product. That would also help passengers calibrate their trust in what the cars can actually do.

According to recent reports, “We’re much more accepting of technology when we have a better understanding of its limitations,” he noted. “Under-promising and over-delivering always wins.”.

The stakes are particularly high for an industry that has already seen how promptly a safety incident can derail a business. In 2023, a Cruise robotaxi dragged a pedestrian who had been struck by another vehicle, prompting California regulators to suspend the firm’s driverless permits. More than a year later, General Motors revealed it would stop funding Cruise’s robotaxi development, citing the cost of scaling the business and growing competition.

“We as humans are enamored by technology, and first impressions do matter,” Reimer remarked. “But at the end of the day, when we experience something that doesn’t feel right, it does erode trust.”.

It has been revealed that reimer also believes Waymo will eventually face a serious incident of its own, given the sheer number of vehicles and miles involved. “It is a law of probabilities,” he stated. “Something will happen at some point.”.

That’s why he worries about companies presenting technology that’s still evolving as something consumers can already trust without hesitation.

“We are talking about a technology that can revolutionarily change how we live and move, but can also suffer from a complete collapse of consumer trust overnight,” Reimer said.

It has been revealed that “Trust is the coveted commodity,” Reimer remarked. “And we are not looking at how to manage trust as effectively as we should.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking firm, has a upcoming CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based tech giant acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software tech giant Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and claims it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Sources indicate that its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli noted Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

In a recent development, zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Industry observers note that zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

According to recent reports, zonar has added 1,000 latest customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli mentioned.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”.

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

According to recent reports, “Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The tech giant cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

#41478. Adecco CEO: Only 19% of workers think their bosses get AI’s toll. This is the leadership test of this generation.

Adecco CEO: Only 19% of workers think their bosses get AI’s toll. This is the leadership test of this generation.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that only 19% of workers say their leaders are empathetic to the effects of change.
  • According to recent reports, the AI debate is entering a more serious phase.
  • It has been revealed that AI’s productivity prize will not come from rolling out more tools alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that only 19% of workers say their leaders are empathetic to the effects of change. That finding, from our latest Global Workforce of the Future research surveying 40,500 workers across 36 countries, should make every leader stop and think.

According to recent reports, the AI debate is entering a more serious phase. The first wave focused on what AI could do. The second focused on massive jobs replacement. What matters now is more pragmatic: which organizations can turn AI into lasting productivity, resilient operating models and better work? How do leaders prepare themselves to accompany their people and organizations to create value?

It has been revealed that AI’s productivity prize will not come from rolling out more tools alone. It will come from redesigning work, skills, governance and operating models. Technology may be the catalyst, but workforce readiness will determine how much value companies actually create.

AI needs to happen with people and not to people. This is the leadership test of this generation.

The evidence gives us reason for optimism, but not complacency. Labor market data tells a more nuanced story than the job apocalypse headlines of earlier this year. AI is not triggering a collapse of human work. It is reshaping how work is organized, performed and governed. Employment remains resilient across most advanced economies – OECD employment rates remain near record highs. Large-scale AI-driven job losses just have not materialized – with impact on tasks rather than jobs. Most companies are still at the beginning of their AI journey, experimenting with tools and trying to understand where value can be created.

According to recent reports, disruption is not insignificant but still far from the scale suggested by some narratives. Entry-level hiring in AI-exposed knowledge work is under real pressure, particularly in software and customer service, but we also see positive signals. Our placement data collected in 23 different markets points to a clear shift in demand: over the past nine months, entry-level placements in AI-exposed functions declined by 2.2% year on year, while demand for highly skilled white-collar profiles rose by 28%. A credible people strategy needs to hold both realities at once: confidence that work is not disappearing at the same time as urgency about how swiftly tasks, skills and career pathways are changing.

Sources indicate that the more important shift is not the replacement of people. It is the redesign of work itself. The organizations that act fastest will turn AI into a lasting competitive advantage.

According to recent reports, history is instructive here. General-purpose technologies like steam power, electricity, and information and communications technology did not transform productivity simply because organizations adopted them. Their value emerged only once businesses redesigned workflows, jobs, skills and management practices around them.

Industry observers note that AI will be no different. Buying technology is relatively easy. Changing how an organization operates is the hard part.

According to recent reports, in terms of work redesign, this requires a shift from workforce management to hybrid workforce orchestration: the discipline of continuously designing, coordinating and evolving work so that people and AI agents contribute where they create the greatest value. Intelligent systems can deliver speed, scale and pattern recognition, while people provide judgment, creativity, trust, accountability and human connection.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 59 out of every 100 workers will need training by 2030. Of those, 29 can be upskilled within their current role, 19 can move into new opportunities with the right support and 11 risk being left behind. That makes the central challenge a strong focus on access to learning while creating robust career pathways. The Adecco Group provides training, upskilling and redeployment services, so we see these transitions up close, every day.

Workforce readiness and cultural resistance are now major barriers to adoption. Overcoming them will be a defining leadership challenge in the years to come.

The stark reality is that many organizations are moving faster with technology than their people’s understanding and confidence, creating a readiness gap that slows transformation and hurts productivity.

Our latest research exposes a striking contradiction at the heart of AI adoption. Three quarters of workers now use AI at work, yet formal training completion has fallen by 10 percentage points in a single year. The workforce is broadly open to change, but organizations are falling short on the conditions that make it possible: only 36% explain to employees how AI creates opportunity for them, and only 39% involve workers directly in job redesign.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits are already becoming unevenly distributed. Workers who have completed AI training are 51 percentage points more likely to feel comfortable working alongside AI, and 96% of those involved in redesigning their roles are willing to adapt to change, versus 29% of those excluded from the process.

Sources indicate that this is the leadership bottleneck in the transition. Just 21% of workers feel concerns about fresh technologies are taken seriously and only 39% feel supported by their manager to adapt.

The implications for the C-suite and investors are significant. AI readiness cannot be measured by technology spend, license numbers or chatbot adoption alone. It must be judged by whether AI is improving productivity, strengthening workforce agility, building trust, increasing skills resilience and helping organizations to redeploy talent as work evolves.

We should therefore stop treating productivity and people as competing objectives. The organizations that succeed will not treat AI primarily as a cost-cutting exercise. They will treat it as an operating model transformation – shaping work around human strengths, involving employees in change, embedding governance and creating continuous systems for learning and mobility.

In a recent development, for investors, this demands a broader definition of AI maturity. Does implementation lead to measurable business impact? Does the organization understand how work is changing? Can it continuously redeploy skills? Can it measure improvements in productivity and work quality, not just headcount reductions? These will increasingly become the leading indicators of long-term resilience.

Leaders need to do three things:.

First, redesign work before automating it. Understand where people create differentiated value and where AI can augment or automate tasks.

It has been revealed that second, build skills around real work and real career opportunities. Training without a pathway to apply those skills will not be enough.

Recent findings suggest that third, involve people in the change. Explain what is changing, listen to concerns and give employees a role in redesigning how their own work gets done.

None of these are technology decisions. They are leadership decisions.

In a recent development, that is why I remain optimistic. The defining capability of the intelligence era will not be artificial intelligence alone. It will be leaders’ ability to orchestrate human and digital intelligence together in ways that make organizations more productive, more resilient and more human. AI is changing how work gets done.

And this, ultimately, is the opportunity in front of us: not simply to deploy AI, but to use it to expand human potential.

#41477. Your Best Employees May Be the Ones Nobody Hears From

Your Best Employees May Be the Ones Nobody Hears From

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything.
  • Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and states very little.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and states very little.

It has been revealed that which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

I’ve led and worked with teams across consulting, technology and marketing, and I’ve learned to be careful about equating confidence with capability. People communicate differently. Some think through problems by talking. Others need time to consider the information before forming an opinion.

Neither approach automatically produces better judgment. But many workplaces reward one more visibly than the other.

In a recent development, think about how most brainstorming sessions operate. A leader presents a problem and asks for ideas. Someone immediately offers a suggestion. Another person agrees, adds something, and the conversation moves forward.

Industry observers note that within minutes, a direction begins to emerge. The session appears productive. People are engaged, ideas are flowing, and decisions are being made.

But whose thinking shaped the outcome?

If the first confident suggestion becomes the foundation for the discussion, everyone else may spend the meeting reacting to that idea instead of considering alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that this is especially problematic when the most senior person speaks first. Employees may hesitate to challenge an executive, even when they recognize a weakness in the proposed approach.

That’s why I prefer giving people the problem to think about before asking them to solve it together. Even a short explanation sent ahead of a meeting can change the conversation. People arrive with their own observations rather than immediately responding to whoever speaks first.

Industry observers note that some employees contribute best through discussion. Others communicate more effectively in writing or smaller groups. A leader who relies exclusively on group meetings may never hear valuable insights from people who dislike competing for attention.

I would build more than one opportunity for participation into important decisions. Ask employees to submit their observations before a meeting. Invite questions afterward. Create smaller working groups when a topic requires deeper thinking.

And when someone who rarely speaks contributes an idea, give it the same consideration you would give a suggestion from your most outspoken colleague.

It has been revealed that the objective isn’t to force quiet employees to become more extroverted. It’s to make sure communication style doesn’t determine whose judgment matters.

According to recent reports, A leader can repeatedly tell employees that every idea is welcome. Those words mean very little if people watch a colleague get embarrassed for disagreeing.

Employees notice how leaders respond to criticism, particularly when the criticism is valid. In my earlier Entrepreneur article about transparent decision-making, I discussed why explaining how decisions are made is essential to building organizational trust.

That principle extends to brainstorming. You don’t need to accept every suggestion. But people should understand why an idea was adopted, rejected or deferred.

If you ask for different perspectives and then consistently reward agreement, employees will eventually stop offering them.

Sources indicate that there is another dimension to this problem. Even when quiet employees perform exceptionally well, their contributions can remain invisible beyond their immediate managers.

They receive positive feedback, but the opportunities that lead to career advancement go elsewhere. I previously explored this distinction between receiving advice and gaining access to opportunity, and it raises a useful question for business owners: Are you developing capable employees, or are you also making sure their capabilities are recognized?

When someone does excellent work, bring that contribution into conversations where decisions about responsibility, promotions and opportunities are being made. Don’t reserve high-visibility assignments for the people who are already comfortable promoting themselves.

Here’s something I would encourage every founder to try.

It has been revealed that think about your last five important team decisions. Who contributed most of the ideas? Whose recommendations shaped the final outcome? Were the same three or four people consistently heard?

Sources indicate that now look at who wasn’t part of those conversations. Were they excluded because they lacked relevant expertise, or because nobody created an opportunity for them to contribute?

You may find that the organization has more insight available than its meetings suggest.

According to recent reports, try rotating who leads discussions. Ask people to share independent recommendations before opening the floor. Review whether important assignments are distributed according to capability or visibility.

These changes don’t require a new leadership program or expensive technology. They require awareness of how influence operates inside your business.

It has been revealed that I’m not suggesting that confident employees should speak less or that every idea deserves equal weight. Organizations need people who can articulate their thinking, make decisions and move work forward.

But confidence should never become a substitute for sound reasoning. The strongest leaders create conditions in which employees can question assumptions without worrying about how that will affect their standing. They also recognize that sometimes the person who speaks last has been thinking about the problem longer than anyone else.

Before your next brainstorming session, consider whether you’re hearing from the people with the most to contribute or simply the people most comfortable contributing.

It has been revealed that your best idea may already be sitting in the room. You might just need to make space for it.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and states very little.

Which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software firm, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

According to recent reports, his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health tech giant Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health prepares that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”.

In a recent development, but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the blueprint.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Recent findings suggest that kelman, by his own account, is fresh to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

It has been revealed that chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software manufacturer he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in latest blood.”.

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

It has been revealed that that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native manufacturer in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn aims to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

Recent findings suggest that A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the tech giant hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a newly introduced mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He noted at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab confirmed new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

Nvidia released a new decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the firm, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia remarked that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.".

Nvidia and IBM also revealed aims for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," mentioned Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

In 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

Tech Report: Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

Sources indicate that according to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Sources indicate that timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

In a recent development, this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

It has been revealed that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Industry observers note that finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Recent findings suggest that contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

According to recent reports, denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

Latest Update: I’m the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally. Here’s what business leaders are wrestling wit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past year, the conversation about enterprise AI and security has fixated on what region the models come from.
  • It has been revealed that what they worry about is more simple.
  • These questions matter more than ever right now, and not just because of the latest string of hacks over the past month, including PHP2Shell which left millions of websites around the world vulnerable, but because of how AI is being used in businesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past year, the conversation about enterprise AI and security has fixated on what region the models come from. It is a fair question. But as the cofounder of the world’s largest platform to run open models locally, I often speak with the increasing number of business leaders adopting open models. Where their models come from is not the question that keeps them up at night.

It has been revealed that what they worry about is more simple. They ask questions like, “Where does my data go when I use these models?”, “Who can see it?”, and “How long is it kept?”.

These questions matter more than ever right now, and not just because of the latest string of hacks over the past month, including PHP2Shell which left millions of websites around the world vulnerable, but because of how AI is being used in businesses. Coding agents, security tools and internal assistants send enormous amounts of manufacturer information to a model: source code, internal documents, customer details, the context of a team’s daily work. Not only is this highly sensitive information for a business, but it’s also extremely valuable to anyone who wants to train a model of their own.

AI leaders are already bracing for what comes next. NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang made it a feature in his keynote at GTC Berlin, and Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer, recently warned that conditions would get worse before they improve, urging business leaders to take action. That action starts with knowing where firm information goes when AI is used.

In a recent development, most companies assume a vendor either protects their data or it doesn’t. The reality is not as black-and-white.

There are cheap, readily available services that openly trade lower prices for the right to train on the data you send. That can be a reasonable deal, as long as the customer knows they are making it. There are also providers that promise zero data retention: prompts and responses are processed, not stored, and never used for training. In between those two, sits a large gray area of providers that promise not to train on your data but may keep it for a number of days.

It has been revealed that none of these are inherently wrong. But in a world where the portion of developers that use coding agents seems to be heading toward 100%, enterprise leaders need to understand the risks of an agent acting on a developer’s behalf. An agent can end up on the wrong end of that provider spectrum, without any developer actually deciding to put them there. As demand for tokens has surged, providers have taken on more traffic. Not all of them have built the controls to match.

Enterprises should treat data retention the way they treat any other vendor risk: ask the question directly, get the answer in writing, and make zero retention the default.

Sources indicate that then there’s the question about models. American or Chinese? Closed or open? Open models have historically been framed as less secure, but in practice, many enterprises find the opposite. Companies can run them in their own environment, so data never leaves. Or they can run them with a provider they trust, in a region their compliance teams have approved. Either way, the tech giant chooses where its data goes.

In a recent development, menlo Ventures’ latest data on the state of AI in the enterprise reported that open-source models’ share of usage is on the rise, suggesting significant future growth. About 10 million developers around the world use Ollama every month to run open models, processing trillions of tokens per day. Eighty-five percent of Fortune 500 companies have Ollama installed on desktops to run open models locally. They’re integrating open models into their workflows for a variety of reasons, among them open models’ lower costs and superior or equal performance on most software development tasks. On coding tasks, for example, the open source model DeepSeek V4 Flash scores within 0.6 points of Anthropic’s Opus 5, at about 1/13 of the cost.

In a recent development, A fintech firm we work with told us that they’d burned 60% of their annual budget three months into a contract with a frontier model. Eighty-five percent of that spend came from engineers defaulting to the most expensive models, leading them to test open models for about a year. On code review, an open model (Deepseek) was faster and cheaper than Anthropic’s Sonnet. Across routine engineering work, open models performed essentially the same as Anthropic models. After two weeks routing most engineering work to open models, while still keeping frontier models for complex problems, they saw an immediate 30% savings on token costs.

Another one of our customers, a large consumer AI company, was spending more than $10 million on frontier models. In their own (human) evaluation, an open model (Gemma 4) matched the frontier model they were using at roughly 1/10th of the cost.

Open models are also becoming a practical tool for defense. Security teams need to work closely with the techniques attackers use: analyzing malicious code, probing their own systems, responding to an incident in real time. Access to that kind of capability on closed models can be limited to specific programs controlled by the labs that build them, where open models are available to any team that needs them.

Of course, open models are not immune to misuse, but the answer isn’t to leave defenders without options. It is to run them carefully, on infrastructure you trust, with clear rules for your data. Even the labs say so. Anthropic’s S-1 filing acknowledges that cyber and safety risks may delay the release of its most capable models. That can be a responsible choice, but it means defenders who depend on a single gated provider can find themselves without access when they need it most.

It has been revealed that models have advanced faster than most corporate AI policies. Many companies that were wary of open models a year ago are now comfortable with them, including models developed outside the United States, provided they run on US or European infrastructure under strict data terms. Their policies should catch up to that reality. Three questions are a good place to start:.

In a recent development, AI is becoming part of nearly every workflow in the enterprise. The companies that handle it well will not be the ones that picked the “right” model. They will be the ones that stayed in control of their data.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a company they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

In 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I debuted in a market already crowded with established competitors.

Every time I’ve started a fresh business, I’ve faced the same challenge: Why should anyone trust a manufacturer they’ve never heard of?

You can tout the quality of your product and its reliability all you want. You can use words like “leading” or “best-in-class” on your social media and website. But as it’s commonly stated: talk is cheap. You may know your claims are true, but how do you get someone else to believe them?

In a recent development, it starts with a product that keeps its promises, so well that customers are willing to vouch for you. To reach the next level, you need credible third parties to back you up, too. Once you have all this, you have to raise your visibility.

None of this is easy, and you can’t skip any steps. Here’s what’s worked for me, from building a product people recommend to earning the kind of credibility you can’t buy.

Recent findings suggest that advertising can buy you short-term attention, but a product won’t last long if customers don’t like it or find it useful. If what you offer has serious flaws, word will spread fast.

It has been revealed that here’s the thing: Most founders get this backward. We think about the launch, the website, advertising, PR and growth long before the product lives up to its promises.

According to recent reports, at ZeroBounce, accuracy was the promise everything else depended on. Before we launched, I wanted our email list validation service to reach at least 98% accuracy. It took a lot of testing and plenty of frustrating moments to get there.

It has been revealed that when we launched, the website wasn’t pretty, and the back end left a lot to be desired. But the product was something we could stand behind. We’ve kept raising the bar since then. Today, we guarantee 99.6% email verification accuracy on most email domains, and we’ve published terms for what happens if we fall short. Your most notable claims should be specific, because they need to be measurable.

Reviews have never been more valuable. We read them before booking a hotel room, ordering virtually any product under the sun and choosing software. Your customers are doing the same research on you. Don’t fear reviews. Embrace them and make them part of your marketing.

It has been revealed that A good review can answer questions your website can’t. Did the product work well? Was support helpful? Did the customer say that they’d choose the product again?

According to recent reports, but here’s what takes many founders a long time to learn: Handling praise is easy. Negative reviews are where you have a chance to shine.

Recent findings suggest that that surprises some people. But how you respond when something goes wrong can say more than the review itself. We’ve had upset customers update a one-star review to five stars after seeing our genuine efforts to fix the problem.

Give your satisfied customers a frictionless way to share their experience, and do this early. Pay close attention to what people are saying, especially when the feedback is uncomfortable. Take your ego out of the equation. It isn’t easy, but that feedback is the most valuable information you have for improving your product. You’re also building a public record of how your firm treats people.

Sources indicate that some customers will be unfair. That’s okay. You and your team can show true integrity.

Any company with a budget can throw money at advertising. PR is a different game. To make the news, an editor or producer has to decide you’re newsworthy and that their audience would care. You can’t pay for that. You have to earn it.

ZeroBounce has invested heavily in marketing over the years, but PR builds our credibility in a different way. When a renowned media organization features your manufacturer, the message packs a powerful punch because you can’t pay for it.

The same goes for industry awards and certifications. Security is a big deal for data companies like ours, so we complete annual SOC 2 Type 2 audits and hold ISO/IEC 27001 certification. We’ve also been recognized on national lists of the most successful companies in the U.S.

The point isn’t to collect media and award logos. It’s that there’s tremendous value when a credible organization examines part of your business and puts its own reputation on the line by praising your work.

You can’t assume a great product will find its market on its own.

We’ve tested various marketing channels at ZeroBounce because I wanted potential customers to find us wherever they were looking for a solution to their email marketing problems.

Say a prospect first reads an article about your company. Next, they see your name in search results. Then they visit your website, read customer reviews and look at your social media profiles. People rarely make an important business decision or a significant purchase after one exposure to a company. They research, compare and check the temperature before they decide.

What they’re looking for is consistency across all of those signals. They want to see satisfied customers and signs of trustworthy leadership. You’d be surprised how many online companies don’t have a single person’s name attached to them. You need an active presence and consistent information. Every box you check removes a little more uncertainty and earns a little more trust.

Recent findings suggest that if someone hears about your organization today, they may check out your company’s LinkedIn before they ever speak with your sales team. They’ll notice the language you use to describe the business, the kind of people who work there and what you publish. They’ll also notice whether customers engage with you and whether the company seems active. Have you ever visited a company’s LinkedIn page and found that its last post was a year and a half ago? What impression does that leave with you?

For B2B businesses especially, founders should give that presence the attention it deserves. We’ve built ZeroBounce’s presence across all major social media platforms. But two to three years ago, we looked closer at our metrics and we realized LinkedIn is where we should put most of our focus.

In a recent development, putting our time and attention into LinkedIn has paid off: our community and engagement began to grow, and now we’re exploring upcoming ways to reach more people. Our next step is to upgrade to a Premium Manufacturer Page.

The credibility features caught my attention. A LinkedIn Premium Manufacturer Page would let us feature a customer testimonial prominently and showcase our awards, right where prospects are already checking us out. When people like or comment on our posts, we could automatically invite them to follow the page. We’d also get deeper insight into how people engage with our content and how our page compares with competitors’.

That last part especially interests me — I want to know what catches people’s attention and where we stand against other companies in our space.

Sources indicate that at a certain point, your company may pursue a higher-tier customer, enter into a fresh market, seek investors or become part of an acquisition. When that happens, the scrutiny is dialed up even more.

Decision makers will examine your product, customers and revenue. Everything will get a close look: your leadership, security, reviews, press coverage and how you’ve presented yourself through the years. Many companies try to polish these things right when they need them, when, in reality, their reputation should have been years in the making.

Start with building a product or service that’s worth trusting. Take the very best care of your customers. And let those customers speak. Give credible third parties plenty of reasons to talk about you. Market the business enough that the right people know it exists. And take care with every place a customer might go to look you up.

Trust takes time to build, but you don’t have to figure it out alone. LinkedIn’s latest Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build credibility and reach customers, and LinkedIn’s small business tools can help you strengthen every place prospects look you up.

You don’t need everyone to trust your company. You just need to give the right people enough good reasons to decide that they can.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a firm they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

Recent findings suggest that in 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I launched in a market already crowded with established competitors.
