by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA stated Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA noted Tuesday.

Sources indicate that in its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA mentioned it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA mentioned. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

Sources indicate that ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”.

Sources indicate that impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

It has been revealed that amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller remarked before the flight.

According to recent reports, before Sunday, Amazon had released 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Industry observers note that amazon has said it intends to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Sources indicate that the Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) revealed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Industry observers note that notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

Sources indicate that as per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

It has been revealed that during the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In a recent development, in its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#41466. GoDaddy chief strategy and legal officer: AI agents still have a trust problem. The solution is waiting

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (756 w)

GoDaddy chief strategy and legal officer: AI agents still have a trust problem. The solution is waiting

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the age of AI assistants is almost here.
  • Recent findings suggest that that convenience could transform the digital economy.
  • The answer will shape whether the next generation of the internet remains open and interoperable—or becomes fragmented across a handful of competing platforms and proprietary ecosystems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the age of AI assistants is almost here. Soon, we’ll delegate tasks like comparing flight prices or managing routine household purchases to agents acting on our behalf.

Recent findings suggest that that convenience could transform the digital economy. But it also raises a basic question. How will those systems know which agents, services, and businesses they can trust?

The answer will shape whether the next generation of the internet remains open and interoperable—or becomes fragmented across a handful of competing platforms and proprietary ecosystems.

We have solved a problem like this before. In the early days of the internet, navigating online was like trying to find a business in a city with no street names or storefront signs. The destinations existed. But users needed to know the underlying IP address of each server.

Sources indicate that the Domain Name System, or DNS, changed that. It transformed the internet from a confusing network of numerical addresses into a navigable web of trusted identities. Endings like .com, .gov, and .edu helped organize the landscape. More importantly, websites could present stable, human-readable names of their own.

Names like Wikipedia.org and Amazon.com told customers exactly where they were going. These names also gave businesses and institutions a unique, durable, and universally accessible online presence, one which many built into the global brands we recognize today.

In a recent development, DNS also helped establish trust. Without such a system, a name like Amazon.com could never have functioned as a trusted commercial identity. A user might have seen the label in a browser and still had little basis for knowing whether it pointed to Amazon’s servers or to a convincing imitation run by fraudsters.

We are approaching a similar inflection point with AI agents. As these systems increasingly operate autonomously on the web, they will need a shared way to know who—and what—they are dealing with.

Industry observers note that in effect, the internet needs an identity layer for agents. At GoDaddy, we contributed to the open standard—Agent Name Service, or ANS. And since the DNS already does this for web and email services, it can readily adapt to do the same for AI agents.

In practical terms, ANS—now a Linux Foundation project—would help AI agents distinguish legitimate services from convincing imposters before moving money, sharing data, or completing transactions. It would give agents a public way to identify one another, verify who stands behind them, and confirm what they are authorized to do.

Recent findings suggest that that is crucial. An AI travel agent must be able to confirm that it is interacting with an airline’s legitimate booking system, not a polished imitation. An AI shopping agent needs to verify that the merchant, payment processor, and delivery provider are authentic before placing an order.

The risks extend beyond outright fraud. Imagine a firm using an AI procurement agent to evaluate suppliers. A supplier could purchase that agent, keep the software and domain name the same, and nudge the AI to recommend its own products.

To the business using the agent, nothing appears to have changed. But the AI is no longer acting entirely in the customer’s interest.

Without a shared identity and verification layer, businesses may have no reliable way to detect those shifts—and ensure that their agents are doing the work they expect them to.

ANS allows every business to verify who operates an AI agent, whether its software matches its registered version, and whether its ownership or software has changed.

Some companies are already building ways for agents to communicate with one another, especially in payments and logistics. But interoperability inside a handful of commercial ecosystems is not the same thing as a global open standard for machines to follow.

According to recent reports, if machine identity is left to a patchwork of proprietary protocols, the agent economy will grow inside private silos. One organization’s agents will work best with its preferred merchants, payment providers, and service platforms.

In a recent development, the internet we know and use today evolved thanks to shared infrastructure that no one company controlled. The next phase of the internet will require the same openness.

Without a common identity layer for AI agents, the promise of the agent economy will give way to confusion and fraud. And we’ll still be spending hours trying to find the best deal on plane tickets.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella stated the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

It has been revealed that “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

It was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

How to Spot Employee Burnout Before the Holiday Rush Takes Its Toll

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that for a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief.
  • Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that for a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

It has been revealed that that is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

Sources indicate that the right workforce technology helps owners see that pressure building. Connecting scheduling, timekeeping and payroll information makes it possible to spot recurring workload problems, understand who is affected and adjust coverage before another request to stay late becomes the only solution.

UKG’s 2025 Retail Workforce Report found that only 18% of retailers anticipated employee burnout as a major challenge. Meanwhile, UKG’s 2025 global study of frontline workers found that 76% of frontline employees reported feeling burned out at work.

Underestimating that strain can lead an owner to strategy for holiday sales the team cannot sustainably support. Earlier visibility into workload gives owners time to arrange coverage before that cycle begins.

It has been revealed that small business leaders often work alongside their employees and know them well. Yet familiarity can make a staffing problem harder to recognize. It has been revealed that disconnected systems make that pattern easier to miss. A schedule indicates a filled shift, while payroll records the extra hours after they have been worked. Overtime is one of the most crucial workforce operations signals because it shows where demand and workforce capacity are no longer aligned. Occasional extra hours may be welcome for some, but repeated overtime concentrated among a few employees warrants a closer look, especially when their schedules also leave little time between shifts.

Imagine a small retailer whose most experienced associate regularly stays an hour past her scheduled finish. Each request seems reasonable in isolation. Over three weeks, however, she also covers two absences and works several closing shifts followed by early openings. The owner sees someone dependable; the combined records reveal the true cost of how much additional work she is carrying.

In a recent development, connected timekeeping and scheduling tools can make that cumulative demand visible without requiring the owner to reconstruct it from old schedules and messages. Alerts about approaching overtime or short intervals between shifts give a manager a chance to discuss coverage before publishing the next schedule.

In a recent development, attendance changes add another piece of context. If absences rise on a team that has been working extra hours, the combination is worth exploring. While data alone does not establish that someone is burned out, it helps managers ask better questions about workload and support.

This is where workforce analytics earns its value for a lean business: It helps owners manage workforce operations proactively rather than reactively. Effective workforce operations requires connecting labor demand, staffing levels, scheduling, attendance, timekeeping and employee experience data to create a complete picture of how work gets done. When leaders can see those connections, they can intervene before a staffing challenge becomes an operational disruption.

Sources indicate that holiday staffing decisions often start with last year’s sales, but sales alone cannot explain why a team keeps falling behind. A store may have enough labor hours for the week and still depend on employees staying late because coverage does not line up with the work. That mismatch can turn an otherwise manageable holiday workload into a recurring source of exhaustion.

Consider a shop where afternoon pickup orders regularly arrive while employees are unloading a delivery. To an owner reviewing weekly totals, the overtime may suggest the store simply needs more hours overall. Connecting order activity, labor demand, scheduling and timekeeping data can reveal a workforce operations problem that would otherwise remain hidden.

Sources indicate that with demand forecasting and scheduling technology, that pattern can inform the next schedule. AI-assisted scheduling can help identify an employee with the right skills and availability, reducing the time the manager spends working through possible changes.

The benefit is that the closing team no longer has to absorb the same unfinished work night after night. Addressing the bottleneck earlier can make finishing on time more predictable, giving employees greater confidence in their schedules. For the owner, it also creates a clearer basis for deciding whether to move existing coverage or invest in additional hours.

That distinction matters during a season when employees may be balancing holiday expenses with family responsibilities. An automatic reduction in hours could create a different source of stress. Current availability and employee preferences help managers respond to what people actually need.

In UKG’s 2025 retail survey, 86% of retailers mentioned frontline employees wanted more flexibility than their organizations provided. For small businesses, delivering that flexibility can be difficult when every change requires phone calls, group texts and a manager to coordinate the exchange.

Scheduling rules can help check that replacement coverage meets role requirements and flag potential overtime. Industry observers note that the benefit goes beyond convenience. Someone who can resolve a scheduling conflict has more control over how work fits into life outside it. When employees see that technology makes those adjustments easier, they have a concrete reason to trust its role in the workplace.

In a recent development, small businesses rarely have someone available to spend hours analyzing workforce reports. Technology is more useful when it brings a developing problem to the manager’s attention and makes the next decision easier, such as highlighting an open shift alongside qualified employees who are available to work.

Timing determines how many options remain. A coverage gap identified before next week’s schedule is published may be addressed through a voluntary shift change or additional staffing. The same gap discovered during a rush is more likely to land on whoever is already there.

Industry observers note that managers need that support themselves. UKG’s retail report found that 31% of retailers said managers worked additional shifts when understaffed. Industry observers note that keeping demand forecasts and schedules connected also matters after peak sales pass. Returns and inventory work can continue into January, and a smaller team may still face a substantial workload. A successful holiday season depends on having a workforce that can sustain the work and the operational visibility to support it. Burnout, absenteeism, overtime, scheduling conflicts and staffing shortages are often treated as separate challenges, but they are all connected workforce operations signals.

Industry observers note that when small businesses bring those signals together, they gain a clearer understanding of how work gets done across the organization. Workforce operations technology provides the visibility needed to identify strain early, align staffing with demand and respond before employee pressure becomes an operational problem.

Ultimately, organizations that manage workforce operations effectively are better positioned to support their people, serve customers consistently and perform through the busiest times of the year.

But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path highlights how far the probing went.

Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

In a recent development, the loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

Recent findings suggest that that arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

In a recent development, loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale states its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

According to recent reports, so the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Recent findings suggest that loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

Industry observers note that the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

According to recent reports, the loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem reveals pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

An obscure Marxist critic who died fleeing the Nazis saw ‘aura farming’ coming 90 years ago—and why you can’t afford to see the Knicks or Taylor Swift

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gen Z calls it “aura farming.” Live Nation calls it “being there.” The hottest idea in the AI economy belongs to a Marxist critic who wrote his ideas in exile, never saw a royalty, and died tragically—a total obscurity in his own time.
  • Walter Benjamin was obsessed with the subject of the “aura” in the 1930s, and he thought mass reproduction would kill it.
  • “That which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art,” he wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gen Z calls it “aura farming.” Live Nation calls it “being there.” The hottest idea in the AI economy belongs to a Marxist critic who wrote his ideas in exile, never saw a royalty, and died tragically—a total obscurity in his own time.

Walter Benjamin was obsessed with the subject of the “aura” in the 1930s, and he thought mass reproduction would kill it.

“That which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art,” he wrote. “Even the most perfect reproduction of a work of art is lacking in one element: its presence in time and space, its unique existence at the place where it happens to be.”.

His 1935 essay, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” was barely seen during his lifetime, and picked up increasing steam in the ensuing decades, at first in leftist European journals and then its 1968 English translation. Hannah Arendt, a great journalist and critic in her own right, who coined the phrase “the banality of evil” and covered Adolf Eichmann’s trial for the Newly introduced Yorker, selected it for the collection Illuminations, and wrote the introduction.

Recent findings suggest that the German-Jewish critic fled Germany in 1933 and spent most of the rest of the decade in exile, much of it in Paris, working on an unfinished history of the city’s 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades, forerunners of the mall. (He was really into arcades.) In September 1940, he crossed the Pyrenees into Spain with a small group of refugees. Franco’s police told them they would be sent back to France, and the next morning Benjamin was found dead in his hotel in Portbou. His death was officially ruled a suicide, although locals have long questioned that. The rest of his group was allowed to continue into Spain the next day.

Now Benjamin is moving from the lecture hall to the analyst notes and earnings calls.

Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino had a Benjamin-ian quote earlier this month.

“In a world of endless screens and AI-generated everything, the one thing that can’t be replicated is being there,” he mentioned on Nov. 5, as the concert giant reported third-quarter revenue of $10.1 billion, up 19% from a year earlier, on fan attendance of 61 million, also up 19%. Through October, it had sold 170 million tickets—already ahead of all of last year.

“In a world of endless screens and AI-generated everything, real-world experiences become even more valuable,” a spokesperson for Live Nation told Fortune. “You can’t stream or replicate the energy of thousands of fans singing together as they watch their favorite artist. Being there in person is irreplaceable, and that’s driving global demand for live music.”.

For executives and investors, the aura is becoming one of the few things AI can’t make cheaper, and money is following it into live seats, sports teams, and the top of the art market: anything with a time and a place attached.

Dictionary.com defines the TikTok trend of “aura farming” as “doing things with deliberate coolness, confidence, or mystique.” It went viral in 2025 with a video of an Indonesian boy dancing on the bow of a racing boat.

Benjamin’s argument starts with the original. Authenticity, in his definition, is everything a thing carries “from its beginning, ranging from its substantive duration to its testimony to the history which it has experienced.”.

A copy can carry the image but not that history: “The presence of the original is the prerequisite to the concept of authenticity,” he wrote.

Sources indicate that he split art’s value in two. “Cult value” belonged to the original made for ritual, which he wrote “would seem to demand that the work of art remain hidden.” “Exhibition value” belonged to whatever could be shown to as many people as possible.

“In photography, exhibition value begins to displace cult value all along the line,” he wrote.

In a recent development, with generative AI pushing exhibition value close to zero—a chatbot can turn out a passable image, song, or article in seconds—the premium moves to whatever exhibition can’t deliver. Cult value and exhibition value are therefore differentiators in the AI economy.

The art market demonstrates the split. Global art sales rose 4% to an estimated $59.6 billion in 2025, still below their 2022 peak, according to the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026. At auction, growth was concentrated at the top. The value of fine-art lots over $1 million rose 21%, and sales above $10 million rose 30%, while sales under $50,000 fell 2%. Online sales, where art is seen as an image on a screen, fell to $9.2 billion, their lowest level since 2019.

Industry observers note that sports show it, too. A franchise is about as close to Benjamin’s “testimony to the history which it has experienced” as anything that trades. Private equity deals for teams went from 50 in 2018 to 192 in 2025, according to a Goldman Sachs Private Wealth Management report Fortune covered in October. The Los Angeles Lakers were valued at $360 million in 2000 and sold at a $10 billion valuation in 2025, per PitchBook data reported by Fortune’s Term Sheet. Streaming now holds about 20% of the sports media market, up from 8% in 2021, Goldman’s report further found.

There are only 30 NBA teams and a fixed number of courtside seats, and the Fresh York Knicks historic title in 2026, their first in 53 years, came with eyewatering price tags. On TickPick, the cheapest seats for Games 3 and 4 at Madison Square Garden went for $3,876 and $3,609, the most expensive NBA Finals tickets on record, Inc. reported. The aura was just too valuable.

Taylor Swift showed how far fans will go for the real thing. Her Eras Tour grossed an estimated $2.2 billion across 149 reveals from November 2022 to December 2024 and sold just over 10 million tickets, the Associated Press reported, citing Pollstar—the highest-grossing tour of all time. It got significant enough for the Federal Reserve to notice. In its July 2023 Beige Book, the Philadelphia Fed passed along a contact’s report that May had been the city’s strongest month for hotel revenue since the pandemic began, “in large part due to an influx of guests for the Taylor Swift concerts in the city,” as Fortune reported. Sports and music tourism is on track to double to about $1.5 trillion by 2032, according to a report Fortune covered in 2024.

In women’s sports, game-day revenue went from 11% of the business in 2022 to 30% in 2026, while sponsorship fell from 64% to 45%, according to Goldman’s report.

Industry observers note that benjamin wasn’t an aura farmer himself. He thought losing the aura could free art in a Marxist sense, making it accessible to every common man and woman. Mass reproduction, he wrote, “emancipates the work of art from its parasitical dependence on ritual.” He was writing as a man of the left, about politics more than prices.

It has been revealed that recorded music is the original case of mechanical reproduction, and streaming made it close to free, yet what has happened to the industry since illustrates the pull of aura. U.S. vinyl sales grew for a 19th straight year in 2025, passing $1 billion for the first time since 1983, according to RIAA data reported by Music Week. Vinyl brought in more than three times the revenue of CDs. The top seller was Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, at about 1.6 million copies.

Broadway grossed $1.91 billion in the 2025-26 season, up 1% even though the season before ran a week longer, on 14.6 million admissions, the Broadway League stated.

Sources indicate that and writing, the thing AI copies most easily, now comes with a certificate. The Authors Guild introduced a “Human Authored” mark in January 2025 for books whose text was written by people, and opened it to the public in March 2026 at $10 a book for nonmembers.

It has been revealed that “Readers have the right to know if a text was written by AI or a human,” the Guild mentioned. That’s Benjamin’s “presence of the original,” sold as a $10 sticker.

Rapino’s betting that it keeps speeding up. Live Nation expects nearly 180 million fans in 2026, and Rapino stated the manufacturer is “on track to deliver another record year and sustain double-digit growth for years to come.” Benjamin’s essay is still free to download.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

According to recent reports, in his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet remarked that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating fresh ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," remarked Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a latest cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz noted it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

In a recent development, "It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz mentioned.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer stated in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation firm toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

According to recent reports, chew noted his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Industry observers note that chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he noted. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

According to recent reports, the job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he mentioned.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew noted.

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

According to recent reports, on the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and noted, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew mentioned, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew remarked he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he remarked. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he stated.

Unless you’re building a data center or have a side hustle, you’re significantly worse off than last year, according to the Fed

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that walk into a grocery store, park, or gas station, and you’ll notice prices across the U.S.
  • The affordability conundrum facing households is therefore twofold: Not only are prices rising quicker than consumers can reasonably expect, but any increases to their income are coming in well short of the latest demands on their purse strings.
  • The Fed minutes from the meeting ending October 28 read that most participants “judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the committee’s 2% inflation objective.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that walk into a grocery store, park, or gas station, and you’ll notice prices across the U.S. keep climbing. On top of that, the Federal Reserve’s latest minutes suggest that unless you’re in two very niche groups of consumers, you’re probably markedly worse off in terms of income in 2026 compared to last year.By its very nature, inflation erodes spending power as prices rise. But in a balanced economy, when inflation is at its target of 2%, those increases are offset by income growth, so consumers can still afford goods and services without seeking additional income or eating into their savings.But in 2026, inflation has been well above the 2% target. The latest inflation readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics came in at 3.7% over the past 12 months, through September 2026. However, in addition to prices rising above the central bank’s 2% target, Fed minutes from the latest Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting highlighted wage growth for most industries lagged well behind price increases.

The affordability conundrum facing households is therefore twofold: Not only are prices rising quicker than consumers can reasonably expect, but any increases to their income are coming in well short of the latest demands on their purse strings.

The Fed minutes from the meeting ending October 28 read that most participants “judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the committee’s 2% inflation objective.”.

Some sectors are posting wage growth, the notes adding many members “observed that shortages of skilled workers needed for data center construction and related industries had contributed to sizable wage premiums in those industries, while a few noted that reduced labor supply in industries reliant on immigrant workers could add to sectoral wage pressures, although these developments did not appear to be having a material effect on aggregate wage measures.”.

These factors are potentially good news for the Fed because they suggest the U.S. is not on the cusp of an inflationary wage-price spiral—making it easier for the FOMC to bring inflation back to its mandated 2% target. A wage-price spiral refers to a feedback loop in which higher labor costs push up production and consumer demand, leading workers to demand higher incomes again to offset the increased cost of living.

However, while it’s one less headache for the Fed, incomes lagging inflation by nearly 2% means consumers already stretched are being spread even thinner.

In a recent development, “Fed members acknowledged that wage growth is consistent with their inflation target—but inflation is not consistent with their target,” noted UBS’s Paul Donovan to clients this morning. “This is a subtle way of saying that wages are falling behind inflation.”.

Recent findings suggest that but in addition to the industries benefiting from the AI infrastructure boom, Donovan points out that the Fed’s notes convey that “consumer resilience continues to depend on lowering savings rates and engaging in side hustles. It implies labor cost pressures are not an inflation driver.”.

It has been revealed that the Fed has a few weeks and a handful of data releases before its next rate-setting meeting in December. However, the meeting notes state that the economy is “stable and close to maximum employment” while inflation is ahead of target; this suggests tensions in the Fed’s mandate may call for a rate hike.

Industry observers note that interest rate traders assign a 91% probability of a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting, per CME’s FedWatch. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has gone so far as to call for a 50 basis point increase, saying the central bank needs to “shock people.”.

Higher borrowing rates and tighter financial conditions would put further pressure on consumers and the wider economy, a worry for Donovan. He noted that inflationary concerns “focus on oil prices (which the Fed cannot influence) and perhaps AI-related demand (largely beyond the Fed’s reach). The only way to offset those would be to create near-recessionary conditions in the parts of the economy that respond to Fed action.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech.
  • The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.

Recent findings suggest that seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD mentioned in a blog post last week.

According to recent reports, it’s a significant upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD mentioned a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

In a recent development, the only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

Industry observers note that boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Recent findings suggest that police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

It has been revealed that back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a newly introduced name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that good morning. Founded just five years ago, Anthropic is a powerhouse in AI. Now, it’s making its public debut on Nasdaq.

It has been revealed that the company is expected to start trading today under the ticker ANT, with the deal expected to close on Friday. Anthropic declared yesterday that it had priced its IPO at $83 per share, with 980 million shares on offer—about 956.4 million from the company and 23.6 million from existing shareholders.

The offering price is above the initially indicated range of $70 to $78 per share and values the AI manufacturer at $1.5 trillion, Fortune’s tech editor Alexei Oreskovic writes. The company stated it will receive no proceeds from existing shareholders’ sales. Underwriters have 30 days to buy up to 147 million additional shares.

Founded in 2021 and led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic develops the Claude family of AI models and products, including Claude Code and Cowork. Krishna Rao joined Anthropic as the manufacturer’s first CFO in May 2024.

The offering also gives some of Anthropic’s seven cofounders an opportunity to sell a portion of their holdings. Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei, and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan are among those selling small portions of their equity, Oreskovic reports. Read more here.

Recent findings suggest that accelerating growth in its enterprise business is a priority for the manufacturer. “Since Anthropic was founded, we have focused on building AI for the enterprise,” Rao wrote in a LinkedIn post in September. He added: “We will keep building for the use cases that matter most to businesses.”.

It has been revealed that according to Anthropic’s IPO disclosures, as of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 customers had generated at least $100,000 in revenue for the company over the preceding 12 months. That included more than 1,900 customers generating at least $1 million each.

For Rao, financing that growth means securing the computing capacity needed to sustain it without allowing infrastructure commitments to overwhelm the business.

Some investors are making a long-term case for investing in Anthropic. “It may not make money until 2030, and the valuation is enormous,” investor Kevin O’Leary posted Tuesday on X. “But you’re investing in the role AI could play across all 11 sectors of the economy. We’re already seeing AI improve productivity and margins, and Claude has become a major enterprise platform.”.

Meanwhile, Pierre Baqué, CEO and co-founder of engineering AI software company Neural Concept, told me in an email that everyone is focused on Anthropic’s IPO valuation, but the most overlooked aspect is its governance. The founders’ voting power and the Long-Term Benefit Trust’s board-selection rights, he argued, give management more room to prioritize AI safety and long-term goals over short-term financial results.

Investors will certainly be watching both Anthropic’s financial returns and how its governance commitments hold up under public-market pressure.

Sheryl EstradaSheryl.Estrada@fortune.com.

Industry observers note that erik Uitenbogaart was named vice president of finance and CFO at Citgo Petroleum Corporation, (No. 24) effective Nov. 16. Uitenbogaart joins Citgo from LyondellBasell, where he held roles of increasing responsibility since 2013, most recently as vice president of finance, strategy and M&A for Sustainable Solutions. He previously led LyondellBasell’s global financial planning and analysis organization. Before that, he served as controller for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Univar Solutions and spent more than 15 years at PricewaterhouseCoopers.

Repetto previously led bank treasury strategy at BlackRock’s Financial Markets Advisory group, served as chief client officer at Milepost Capital Management, and was a member of the executive operating committee at Promontory Financial Group, an IBM Consulting tech giant. He began his career at Merrill Lynch in 1989 and subsequently held senior roles at Salomon Brothers, JPMorgan, PNC, CRT Capital Group, and Citadel Securities. Repetto brings more than 35 years of experience working with global banks, community banks, and credit unions.

Sources indicate that jesús Rueda Molins was named CFO at Teciem, a provider of treasury and capital markets software. Rueda Molins joins from Apax, where he was a principal on the technology team. Earlier in his career, he worked in McKinsey & Firm’s corporate finance and strategy practice. He has worked closely with Teciem and its leadership team over the past two years and will relocate from New York to London for the role.

Gallup’s latest report suggests that AI is changing specific tasks faster than it is transforming the workday as a whole. Frequent AI use reached 32% of U.S. employees in the third quarter of 2026.

However, an additional finding is 78% report no change in time spent collaborating with colleagues, and 65% say their jobs require the same mental effort. Just 29% of employees in AI-adopting organizations say the technology has raised expectations for daily output.

Taken together, the findings point to a gap between making individual tasks more efficient and redesigning work to translate those gains into broader organizational change.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC claims user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

Industry observers note that on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

Sources indicate that MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange states it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

Sources indicate that the other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN notes the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

According to recent reports, on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN indicates MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

According to recent reports, iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN states the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

It has been revealed that one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Industry observers note that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Industry observers note that predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

Recent findings suggest that finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Industry observers note that three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon’s CEO Andy Jassy has one go-to interview question, and if you can’t answer it on the spot, he’ll look down at his watch and end the interview. At least, according to Bing Gordon.

Gordon was a founding exec at $55 billion EA Games—where he helped create The Sims, the game that had millennial girls around the world hooked—and Audible. He also served on Amazon’s board of directors from 2003 to 2017.

And one time, he was sitting at dinner with fellow Amazon execs, including Jassy before he became chief exec, when the conversation turned to who had the best go-to interview question.

“My go-to interview question is, ‘What would it take to keep you in a firm like ours for 20 years? And who’s your business hero?’ And Andy Jassy had a better one,” Gordon told Fortune. “He said, ‘Mine is: what’s your strategy for constant learning?’”.

Gordon instantly listed the various ways he learns, from reading books to watching people—which Jassy mentioned was an instant green flag.

“He stated: ‘Good, you know it off the top of your head. When I ask that question, if somebody goes, what do you mean? He says, as far as I’m concerned, the interview is now over, and I look at my watch and try to figure out how to get out of it.’”.

Fortune reached out to Amazon for comment.

Gordon, who has just published a book, Everybody Wins, on what games and decades in Silicon Valley taught him about leadership, has some advice for getting ahead of an interviewer’s make-or-break question. “My advice to kids is, you know that in the interview process everybody who is interviewing you has an interview strategy they do again and again and again,” he mentioned. “So take control of the interview.”.

According to recent reports, how? Just outright ask the hiring manager at the start of the interview what their go-to question is—and what they’re looking to learn from that.

Industry observers note that “Just say, ‘I know you have one.’ Let’s talk as peers about the interview process because, frankly, I’m interviewing you as well. So I want to know how you decide who ought to be here.”.

The second question to ask, after “What’s your go-to interview question?” is: What’s the best performance you’ve ever seen in this job, either at your tech giant or in a company like this, and why?

“Now you’ve done two things: You’ve made the interviewer think because nobody’s ever asked him that before. You’ve also communicated in a really nice way that you have high standards, and you want to know what the best is because you’re going to try to get there.”.

And finally, come extra prepared. Gordon borrows a rule from advertising legend David Ogilvy: “Know more about the client’s business than anyone else in the room, including the client CEO.”.

Even if you get the job, Gordon says twenty-somethings should be “highly prepared” if they want to keep impressing their boss, including coming to their first day of work with a one-year plan of action.

“If you want to get promoted in your 20s, which is the top 10% every year, always ask good questions, always have an idea, know as much about the topic as everybody in the room, always get your job done and always know what the A plus is.”.

Gordon and Jassy aren’t the only leaders with signature questions.

IBM’s president Dave McCann asks candidates whether they think we’re in an AI bubble. “Right now I must tell you, I’m always asking candidates if they think we’re in an AI bubble or not,” he stated at the Fortune CEO Forum. “We’ll see how long that question lasts.”.

Industry observers note that there’s no right or wrong answer. McCann doesn’t mind which side you pick, as long as you’ve thought it through.

It has been revealed that linkedIn’s Sue Duke asks candidates what they’d do with the platform’s data. “If you had all of that data and all of our economists and data scientists with you in the morning, what’s the one thing you would want us to do with the graph to have a real impact out there in workers’ lives, in companies’ lives, and in the economy more broadly?” There’s no wrong answer, she said, but she’s looking for “people who dream massive.”.

And some executives are even asking candidates how they’d explain the rules of tennis to a 10-year-old.

It has been revealed that “It’s not one that I came up with, but I heard somebody else ask this very interesting question,” Lilika Beck, president of the $14.5 billion healthcare giant, Sonova, previously told Fortune. “I think what’s cool about that question is it’s a little bit surprising, but it also shows how an individual can simplify and communicate well.”.

Recent findings suggest that others like Bupa CEO Iñaki Ereño and Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler switch up the settings of their interviews to see how candidates act when the hot seat is at a restaurant. Ereño is watching whether the candidate is confident enough to order wine and how they treat the waiter.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Shipchandler interviews senior candidates over 45-minute dinners and listens for how often they say “I.” He also sets aside around 20 minutes for the candidate’s questions. If they have none? “That’s a pretty significant red flag.”.

In a recent development, are you a CEO with a go-to question or an unusual hiring test? Fortune wants to hear from you: Orianna.Royle@fortune.com.
