📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the manufacturer’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” mentioned Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the tech giant’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he remarked.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

Sources indicate that for “advanced” people of each tech giant’s agent tools, it revealed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

According to recent reports, partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The organization is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

Industry observers note that the companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report remarked.

Industry observers note that upcoming MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

It has been revealed that the lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

It has been revealed that microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it indicates matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other upcoming models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

According to recent reports, the other fresh business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Firm consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff revealed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

According to recent reports, the cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Industry observers note that microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature indicates business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

Recent findings suggest that in another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

Industry observers note that almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

The risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets rapidly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

Sources indicate that the Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Recent findings suggest that march 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

Industry observers note that on March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

According to recent reports, the response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

According to recent reports, markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

Industry observers note that the current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

It has been revealed that slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

According to recent reports, the Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

According to recent reports, at the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

Recent findings suggest that but the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. It has been revealed that global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

The hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Sources indicate that mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

Recent findings suggest that one of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the company's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

Sources indicate that the project that won the competition is called Wraps. Its creators are Adarsha Mishra and Hrishabh Ayush. Their project dealt with how to secure user privacy in AI-based transactions. Their project demonstrated a method to prove that search logs were not being saved.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

It has been revealed that founded last year, the firm says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team remarked it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason stated in a statement.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

In a recent development, the newly introduced round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The organization has 13 employees and prepares to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he debuted the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” noted Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, remarked the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

In a recent development, the price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”.

According to recent reports, in the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted.

It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating.

According to recent reports, both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas.

Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks:.

Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Industry observers note that when you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:.

In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:.

It has been revealed that the current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig confirmed that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He said that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

Selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

In a recent development, for some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

Sources indicate that the latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.
  • Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.
  • The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am.

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that states, “Do not search Amazon.”.

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

According to recent reports, for Muse owners, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta rolled out the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas mentioned any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

It has been revealed that what’s newly introduced is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon mentioned it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson stated the manufacturer had nothing to share.

Sources indicate that amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has mentioned Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

Recent findings suggest that on Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Industry observers note that jassy stated Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon rolled out Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak.
  • In a recent development, “We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune.
  • Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million.

In a recent development, “We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.”.

Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew swiftly, until Booking.com and the major hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes noted.

Industry observers note that the founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he noted, referring to the $12.4 million the tech giant had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014.

In a recent development, it was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he stated. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the big one—the manufacturer that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.”.

According to recent reports, leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards to startups as cheap office space. “All this medical stuff was everywhere,” Leathes recalled, and meetings were held in the old operating theater.

Their fifth business idea proved more successful. Motorway, an online marketplace for used cars, was valued at $1 billion in 2001, following a $190 million funding round co-led by Index Ventures and Iconiq Growth. Its 2025 revenue rose 18% to £78 million ($99 million), and its operating losses fell by more than a third to about £22 million ($28 million). Leathes says the company is on track to make its first profit in 2026.

In a recent development, “We learned a massive amount, both through all the companies that had worked, but also the ones that didn’t,” Leathes said. “Those lessons helped us make a lot of the right decisions as we scaled Motorway.”.

Reflecting on the failure of his hotel recommendation app, Leathes said: “What we built wasn’t differentiated enough. If you want to take on Booking.com or Expedia, then you need to rethink the market and build Airbnb, not just a better version of what’s already out there.”.

Industry observers note that with Motorway, the three cofounders took a different approach. By building a marketplace that connects private sellers directly with dealers they were able to cut out the middlemen, Leathes remarked. The car trade “a bit of a graveyard of tech companies coming in thinking they could change it,” he added.

The best-known casualty, online car retailer Cazoo, went public in 2021. It spent heavily on marketing and expansion, then collapsed into administration in 2024.

Sources indicate that motorway took the opposite approach. “We cold-called dealers, stitched deals together on WhatsApp and spent much of our time driving around the country meeting [them],” Leathes mentioned. “That’s how we learned the trade. That’s what taught us what we needed to build.”.

Sources indicate that those early months taught him to let customers shape the business. “It’s the early customers that form the product,” he said. “That means holding the original idea quite lightly and being really willing to drop things that you feel passionate about.” Founders, he added, often need to “pivot really aggressively.”.

According to recent reports, the other lesson was focus. When COVID-19 lockdowns shut Britain’s physical car auctions, dealers flocked to Motorway. The founders raised fresh capital to scale the core business rather than chase newly introduced markets. “If you have something that’s really working, triple down on it,” Leathes mentioned. Nearly a decade in, Motorway still operates only in the UK, although its long-term goal is global expansion.

Sources indicate that leathes said Motorway is open to an IPO but there are no immediate plans. What’s more, London may not be its first choice of listing venue. “At the moment it’s not attractive to scale-ups,” he said. Just eight companies listed in the U.K. in the first nine months of 2026, according to accounting firm EY.

It has been revealed that in Europe, Germany’s Auto1, which also buys cars from private sellers and sells them on to dealers, listed in Frankfurt in 2021. Leathes believes a London float by a homegrown star such as Revolut or Monzo “would definitely help” revive the U.K.’s lackluster market.

Recent findings suggest that but the bar for going public is also shifting. Leathes pointed to the AI boom, led by Anthropic, which this week raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO on record. “This is drastically changing what good looks like in public tech companies,” he said. Investors now measure listings against AI companies growing at extraordinary speed and scale, which makes steady, near-profitable businesses a harder sell.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing users multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Sources indicate that among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

Industry observers note that according to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Recent findings suggest that optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

In a recent development, if successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For owners: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

It has been revealed that jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos mentioned. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”.

In a recent development, nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

Jones mentioned the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place promptly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He remarked he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

In a recent development, nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the Upcoming York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is serving as interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”.

It has been revealed that the Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He stated he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”.

In a recent development, huang himself stated in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the firm.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also stated Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she noted customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”.

Sources indicate that in case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”.

SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • Recent findings suggest that four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • Recent findings suggest that the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Recent findings suggest that four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list claims a lot.

Recent findings suggest that the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets indicates it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule demonstrates up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Recent findings suggest that rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

Industry observers note that the SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

According to recent reports, rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ states a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency aims for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

It has been revealed that commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move promptly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Recent findings suggest that rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that AI is one of the biggest market-moving shifts we have ever seen. Leaders are reorganizing around the technology, latest businesses are being built around the opportunity, and decisions being made about AI today will define our economy for generations.

Industry observers note that I care passionately about seeing more women in leadership, having access to capital, and steering the choices that shape our world. So when I heard AI expert and advisor Allie K. Miller on Emma Grede’s podcast share that women were adopting AI 25% less than men, it stuck with me.

In a recent development, for my whole career, I’ve watched women start a step behind: we still hold only about 29% of C-suite roles and make up fewer than one in five decision-makers at venture firms. Even 2025, a banner year for women-founded startups, tells a misleading story: nearly 41% of the almost $74 billion raised came from two megadeals. Most women founders saw very few of those investment dollars.If women are already underrepresented among leaders, investors, and founders, and now we’re adopting AI more slowly, the gap widens at the exact moment the next generation of business leaders and global decision-makers are being decided.

Industry observers note that concerns around whether AI is ethical or looks like cheating are driving women’s slower adoption, but I also think it comes down to time. We badly underestimate what it takes to carve out hours to learn something newly introduced on top of a full-time job, personal responsibilities, and commitments to friends and loved ones. If I spend a Sunday afternoon building an agent, I’m missing time with my family. The trade-offs are real, and you don’t get that time back.

Recent findings suggest that research suggests the adoption gap may be shrinking, but given how fast AI is moving, incremental progress is not enough. This isn’t a shift women can opt out of. If we want to drive the decisions that will define the next decade, we need to be leading this transformation, not watch it unfold.Here are four things I believe women should focus on right now:.

According to recent reports, I always come back to this line from Ginni Rometty: growth and comfort do not coexist.I’ve seen this firsthand throughout my career: I joined ServiceNow just before COVID hit. Within ten weeks, I went from never having worked from home to doing everything remotely—building relationships, leading a team, and learning dozens of new tools. It wasn’t comfortable, but my team and I adapted. AI demands the same mindset.

In a recent development, the women I see pulling ahead here are the ones who just start using AI before they feel ready or have it all figured out. Getting your hands dirty is the whole point: use AI to analyze a dense report, pressure-test a strategy, or build a simple agent to handle a task you dislike.Pick low-risk moments and let yourself get things wrong. You learn AI by being close to it, not by watching from a distance and waiting until you feel like an expert.

You don’t have to navigate this shift alone. Seek out AI-specific meetups and groups—and connect with professionals who are experimenting in real time and asking the same questions as you.

Industry observers note that it is also worth looking closer to home. Some of our best AI teachers at ServiceNow have been early-career employees who are more comfortable with these tools than others. A little reverse mentoring can go a long way.

Industry observers note that just as importantly, you need to pay it forward. The more women help each other build confidence and capability around AI, the faster we will close the gap. One of the reasons we invited Allie K. Miller to talk about AI and leadership at Knowledge, our annual conference, is that she consistently shares insights that lower the barrier to entry for others.

You can’t be what you can’t see, which is why those of us in senior leadership roles also need to lead by example. When I’m asked how I use AI as a CFO, I’m deliberate about sharing how it has become a real partner in how I work. I want women coming up behind me to see AI fluency as part of their own leadership path, too.

It has been revealed that for much of my career, I was the only woman with a seat at the table. Looking back, I can see how much that proximity shaped my career. Watching leaders like Barry Diller and Dara Khosrowshahi navigate complex, high-stakes decisions taught me lessons no class ever could.It also gave me exposure to projects that prepared me to lead. Before IAC, I didn’t have much M&A experience. There, I learned what a good deal actually looks like, how to think about integration, and the kind of judgment you can only build by doing the work.

Industry observers note that the same principle applies to women and AI right now. Get as close to the AI decision-making as possible. Participate in strategy conversations, use-case assessments, pilots, and learning sessions. Raise your hand for the AI project no one has figured out yet and ask to be in the room where your organization is determining how it will use this technology.

When leadership sees you leaning into the hardest, most key work the tech giant is taking on, you become someone they picture in the next big role.

Understand Your Role in the AI TransformationWe need more than just engineers and programmers working closely with AI.

Industry observers note that to ensure artificial intelligence is as safe, ethical, and effective as it can be, we need people with diverse perspectives and skills working on it. Those with expertise in governance, risk, talent, and change management, for example, have important roles to play in ensuring successful AI deployment at scale.

It has been revealed that at ServiceNow, when we added “AI Enablement” to Jacqui Canney’s title of Chief People Officer, it was done for a reason. AI can’t just be dropped into the tooling mix. People need to understand and learn how to use it well in the enterprise, which means we need to invest in that happening.

We’ve done this in many ways, from company-wide learning sessions, to role-based skills development opportunities through ServiceNow University, to building groups of AI champions that shape how the technology is being used at the team level.

It has been revealed that even the best manufacturer programs won’t do it all for you, though. I always say that no one will care as much about your career as you do, and that’s to no fault of your managers or your company. They may open doors, but you’re the one who must walk through them.

Recent findings suggest that the rooms where AI is being built, deployed, trained, and governed are filling up, and if you’re not in them, those decisions are getting made without you. The time you invest now in learning, the skills you build, and the judgment you develop will compound. As this next era of leadership unfolds, the women who stayed close to AI won’t just be ready for the future; they’ll help define it.

According to recent reports, house of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

In a recent development, HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

This is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake said.

According to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

According to recent reports, ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You noted spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

Recent findings suggest that “The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

Industry observers note that “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and remarked, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that “The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she noted. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

According to recent reports, the region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn remarked, should be judged by the communities themselves.

Recent findings suggest that “And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he remarked. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.

Your Press Page is Rotting. A Yearly Audit Is the Only Thing That Stops It.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A quarter of the web from the last decade has vanished, and two-thirds of links eventually die.
  • A client sent me their press page last spring with some pride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A quarter of the web from the last decade has vanished, and two-thirds of links eventually die. The coverage on your press page is decaying on the same schedule, and a yearly audit is the only thing that stops it.

A client sent me their press page last spring with some pride. Fourteen logos, a decade of coverage, the kind of wall a sales team loves to point at. I clicked through every link while we were on the call. Roughly a third were dead, two more redirected to a publication’s homepage and one article had vanished when the magazine that ran it was sold.

Nobody had done anything wrong. The page simply had not been checked since it was built, and the web had moved on without telling anyone. At ESBO Ltd, the link building and brand mentions agency I run, re-checking the placements we deliver is part of the job, and even so we lose some every year. Coverage is an asset that depreciates, and almost no company books the depreciation.

In a recent development, the scale is documented. When Pew Research Center sampled webpages that existed at any point between 2013 and 2023, 25% were no longer accessible by October 2023. Of pages that existed in 2013, 38% were gone. Nearly a quarter of news webpages contained at least one broken link, and the news sample was not obscure blogs but 2,063 sites a measurement company had classified as news.

Links die faster than pages. Ahrefs tracked links pointing at more than 2 million websites since 2013 and found 66.5% of them had rotted. Almost half of the lost links were dropped because the page or domain carrying them disappeared, and a third were removed by someone editing a page that still exists. Put those two causes together and your coverage is being deleted both by neglect and on purpose.

The causes are rarely dramatic. Publications fold or get sold, and the buyer prunes an archive it never wanted. A redesign migrates the site to a new content system and old addresses stop resolving. An editor runs a cleanup and strips outbound links from older articles, which is the 34% in the Ahrefs data and the one that stings most, because the article survives while your name’s connection to it does not.

Industry observers note that then there is the fine print. Some publishers sell placements with an expiry buried in the terms, and the article comes down on schedule 12 months later. I have written here before about four-figure placements vanishing overnight, but the slow version is more common and nobody notices it, because nobody is looking.

Industry observers note that three things go at once. The search value of the link disappears with the page. The social proof disappears from your press page, replaced by a logo that leads to an error, which is a worse impression on a buyer than no logo at all. And the mention falls out of the layer of the web that AI assistants read live. A system answering a question today can only cite pages that still resolve, so a dead article stops feeding the answer, even if an older training run remembers the name. Everything the mention was doing for you stops on a date nobody told you.

Industry observers note that my own trade does not come out of this well. An agency that sells placements and never re-checks them is selling an asset with an unknown lifespan, and clients should ask about it far more often than they do.

Start by listing every address where your brand appears: the press page, old coverage reports, campaign spreadsheets, the links in your email signatures and investor decks. Most companies have never had that list in one place, and building it is half the value.

Run the list through any broken link checker, then sort the results into four piles. Dead domains, where the publication itself is gone. Dead pages on live sites, where the article was removed or moved. Removed links, where the article stands but no longer connects to you. And redirects, which usually mean a migration that lost your page along the way.

Sources indicate that each pile gets a different response. For a dead page on a live site, pull the copy from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, send it to the editor and ask whether the article can be restored or the reference updated; the hit rate is better than you would expect, because editors dislike broken archives too. For a removed link, ask once and politely, then let it go. For a dead domain, retire the logo from your press page and replace it with coverage that still loads. And for redirects, test whether the fresh address carries the mention, because sometimes it does and the fix is a copy and paste.

Then change how you acquire coverage so the next audit is shorter. Save an archived copy of every new article the day it appears. Before paying any publisher, ask in writing whether the placement is permanent, and treat a vague answer as a no. Put a yearly reminder in the calendar, because this work gets done only when it has a date.

Recent findings suggest that finally, spend on maintenance before you spend on growth. Restoring a mention that already exists costs one email, while earning a new one costs weeks. The press page that impresses a buyer in 2027 will not be the one with the most logos. It will be the one where every logo still goes somewhere, and that is a choice the tech giant makes once a year, with a link checker and an afternoon.

Ledger, a crypto wallet firm, noted it had experienced a security incident related to Optimizely, a third-party service used on its official website, but reassured its customers about the security of their devices and private keys.

In a post, Ledger mentioned it was aware of a security incident impacting Optimizely, a third-party service provider used by many other sites as well.

Recent findings suggest that we are aware of a security incident affecting Optimizely, a third-party service used on https://t.co/d2pWxdG49X, alongside numerous other websites. Our team has remediated the concern, and the malicious code is no longer being served through our website. This incident does not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices. Website optimization platform Optimizely noted it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Optimizely stated that the vulnerable path has now been blocked, the injected code has been removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the issue and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring users that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

Industry observers note that according to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

The main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maybe you have a business idea in your Notes app that you keep thinking about. Or you could be trying to grow a company without letting it take over your life.

Whatever your next challenge looks like, there is something reassuring about learning from authors who have been exactly where you are or conducted research to help you grow.

The best business books show that success is found in the habits people repeat, the conversations they avoid and the attention they give each other.

These books help leaders notice those pivotal moments and make better decisions.

These 10 bestselling books approach business from different directions. Some focus on personal discipline, while others examine trust and creativity. Some were published in the early 20th century, while others debuted last month. They all offer ways to think more clearly about leadership.

Sources indicate that james Clear’s Atomic Habits explains how habits develop and how to redesign routines so good behavior becomes easier. The four rules are to make it obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying. Systems matter more than goals, and repeated actions shape how we see ourselves. For business readers, this is a practical guide to turning ambition into routines. This book has sold more than 30 million copies since its debut nearly a decade ago.

Recent findings suggest that this book, written by Will Guidara, is the story of how exceptional hospitality helped transform Eleven Madison Park into a celebrated restaurant over the course of 11 years. It shows that there is a difference between delivering competent service and making customers feel genuine care. The book describes memorable gestures and close attention to detail in customer interactions. It also showcases a workplace where employees can take initiative and leaders can encourage ownership. The book has sold more than a million copies.

Sources indicate that in this book, David Epstein examines how limits can encourage experimentation and help people solve difficult problems. It draws on research and stories to explore when deadlines, scarce resources and careful boundaries support creativity instead of suppressing it. The question is if constraints help with the task at hand. This is a different way to approach innovation, through clearer boundaries instead of greater resources.

Recent findings suggest that this book was written by former Navy SEAL officers Jocko Willink and Leif Babin, who translate combat leadership lessons into principles for business and everyday work. They say that leaders must take responsibility for their team’s results and not pin the blame on circumstances or other people. This means owning up to mistakes and explaining the mission clearly. They also have to develop a proposal to improve. The biggest takeaway is that accountability begins with the leader’s own behavior.

According to recent reports, ever wanted to learn about leadership through the lives of great presidents? Doris Kearns Goodwin examines leadership through the examples of Abraham Lincoln, Theodore Roosevelt, Franklin Roosevelt and Lyndon Johnson and considers how experience and adversity shaped these presidents. The different crises they went through reveal different ways of responding to uncertainty. The book demonstrates how leaders can adapt when no playbook exists for the situations they are experiencing.

Sources indicate that what do organizations lose when employees feel unable to speak honestly? They may notice a problem, have a useful question or recognize a mistake, yet remain silent because speaking feels like a personally risky move. Author Amy C. Edmondson presents psychological safety as a prerequisite for learning and innovation. She argues that information cannot help an organization if people are afraid to share it. The challenge for leaders is to create an environment where concerns surface early and prompt productive discussions.

Industry observers note that author Adam Grant, who is an organizational psychologist and professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, challenges the tendency to judge people by their starting point. His central argument is that potential depends more on how someone develops and less on where they begin. That shift changes how leaders think about talent because current achievement does not tell the full story of an employee’s future contributions. The book encourages attention to growth rather than fixed assumptions about ability.

Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy.

Sources indicate that economist Joseph Schumpeter, who is often called the “father of entrepreneurship” or the “father of creative destruction,” wrote this book in 1942. In it, he examines how capitalism develops and why it changes societies. The book explains creative destruction, or the notion that innovation replaces established products, businesses and industries rather than just improving them. This is a demanding work of economic and political thought and offers readers a broader understanding of economic disruption.

In this book, which debuted in October, author Christina Wing examines the conversations people avoid even when silence leads to serious consequences. Her subjects include money, retirement, succession, failure, politics and other sensitive complications. She draws on work with family businesses, boards and classrooms to show how fear and secrecy can weaken relationships and delay key decisions. The book offers cases, questions, strategies and scripts for approaching difficult discussions. Its aim is clear communication grounded in empathy and respect.

Recent findings suggest that this recently released book also from author Adam Grant focuses on connection. Why do some relationships deepen while others remain distant? How can people build a stronger sense of belonging? Vibe challenges the idea that meaningful bonds require similar personalities or immediate chemistry. It notes that connections can develop through shared experiences and curiosity. Examples include astronauts learning to trust colleagues they do not like and musicians strengthening relationships through disagreement. The book encourages a more deliberate approach to relationships. People can actively cultivate belonging.
